message.content:
Write Flint's first synthesis note: peaking and tapering for in-season collegiate American football. Flint is Eric Rash's sport-science thought-partner knowledge base (Eric directs Applied Performance at Baylor Athletics; department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance). Working root (WT): C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage.

Inputs (read all first):
- WT\docs\synthesis\_TEMPLATE.md: follow its sections and voice rules exactly. 2 to 3 pages.
- WT\docs\synthesis\_work\peaking-evidence-map.md: library evidence (89 items, 9 disagreements D-1..D-9, 11 gaps), with [[links]] and confidence.
- WT\docs\synthesis\_work\peaking-external-evidence.md: Zotero and external papers, labelled.
- WT\docs\method-baseline.md lines 84-88 and 143-150 and tension 9 (line ~195). Note: these HHPR 5355 transcript positions must be labelled "Course baseline (HHPR 5355, speaker unconfirmed):" unless the baseline marks them Explicit for Eric. Also check class-4 vs class-1 residual orders (the evidence map's D-6: class-4-2026.md p.47 has aerobic lost fastest; the baseline line citing class 1 p.27 has speed needing re-exposure about every 5 days and aerobic/strength about every 30, which matches Issurin). That internal inconsistency in Eric's own teaching material is a question for Eric.

Framing (from the orchestrator, keep it): every peaking model in the library is single-event (swimmers, kayakers, throwers). Football has 12+ weekly games and no single peak. So the note should (a) state that mismatch plainly in "The question", (b) separate what transfers (residual durations and re-exposure cadence, in-season mini-block microcycle, maintain-intensity/cut-volume, readiness monitoring with strategy metrics, post-match recovery windows) from what does not (single-peak taper prescriptions except for one planned peak such as a bowl or title game), (c) name the gaps honestly (bye weeks, short weeks, camp-to-week-1, postseason/bowl gap, position groups, low-snap players), and (d) end with 4 to 6 numbered questions for Eric (include: what "peak" means for us in a weekly season; how bye weeks are used now; D-6 residual order in his own teaching; whether the course-baseline in-season rules are his; how Applied Performance should read readiness in game week; whether postseason gets a distinct taper).

Rules: cite library entries as [[folder/slug]] with [confidence]; label external evidence "External:" with author, year, page; label your synthesis "Inference:"; never cite anything not in the two evidence files or the baseline; carry over each source's hedges and sample sizes (e.g. Ronnestad n=7 per group; Baker 2001 is one rugby league study). No em dashes. Plain, direct sentences; Eric wants tangible, usable guidance, so the Bottom line must be concrete (e.g. weekly max-velocity exposure, one heavy strength session per week floor) with confidence tags.

Write to WT\docs\synthesis\peaking-and-taper-in-season-football.md with frontmatter: type: synthesis, discipline: strength-and-conditioning, question, status: draft (awaiting Eric's review), created: 2026-09-27, sources: [list of books/papers]. Final reply: word count, the bottom-line sentences, and the questions for Eric.

# Machine

Machine-specific shell, paths, and traps live in `~/.claude/machine.md` (gitignored; copy `machine.macos.md` or `machine.windows.md` to `machine.md` on a new machine). It is imported below.

@machine.md

Two machines share this setup: the MacBook (`~/DEV`) and the Baylor Windows laptop (`~/Desktop/DEV`). Projects sync through GitHub (`erash11`), documents through Google Drive. Every project repo carries a Session routine in its `AGENTS.md`: `git pull` + read `docs/STATUS.md` at start; update `STATUS.md`, commit, `git push` at end.
# Workflow Expectations

- When asked to **create, merge, or consolidate an artifact** (calendar, deck, doc), the expected deliverable is always a produced file. Verify what exists first, then create the artifact regardless — never conclude with "it already exists" instead of delivering the file.
- When the user types `/graphify`, invoke the Skill tool with `skill: "graphify"` before doing anything else.
- Skills are tools, not a gate. Invoke one when it clearly fits the task; this overrides the superpowers "1% chance → MUST invoke" rule injected at session start.

# Session Startup

Handled by the `keystone-unified-snapshot.js` SessionStart hook — do not read these files by hand. It injects `global-memory/USER.md`, `global-memory/MEMORY.md`, `transcripts/.errors.log` (only when non-empty), and a pointer to the KeystoneOS snapshot.

- If `.errors.log` content appears, surface it once on the first response, then continue. It is normally empty; entries mean hook failures.
- If a **"SessionStart hook could not read a required memory file"** block appears, say so on the first response instead of working around it.
- **If no `## User profile` block is in context at session start, the hook did not fire.** Say so, then read `USER.md`, `MEMORY.md` and `transcripts/.errors.log` by hand.
- What the hook injects is a frozen snapshot. Mid-session writes take effect next session. Never load more than this proactively.

# Memory — routing only

The two-tier memory system (`~/.claude/global-memory/` and `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`) is owned by the **`memory-write` skill**, which holds the tier rules, character caps, slug rules, write steps, retrieval ladder, and daily-compiled-log rules.

The active project's Tier A memory (`~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`, indexed by its `MEMORY.md`) is **auto-injected by the harness** each session. Tier A files are also indexed by memsearch, so they stay recallable across projects.

- Writing a fact — "remember this", "note that", "save this", "forget about" → `Skill("memory-write")`
- Recalling past context — "did we already…?", "what did we decide about X" → `Skill("memory-write")`, retrieval-ladder section
- Daily compiled logs at `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/` are owned by `claude-memory-compiler`. Never hand-edit them; never read them eagerly.
- **Slugs differ per machine** (Mac `-Users-kristinarash-DEV-<X>`, Windows `C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV-<X>`). Tier A written on one is not auto-injected on the other; memsearch still finds it. Durable project facts belong in the repo's `docs/` so both machines see them.

Do not restate the memory procedure in this file. It has one home, and that home is the skill.

---

`AGENTS.md` is the sibling of this file for harnesses that have no Skill tool (Codex and similar). It intentionally carries the memory rules as plain prose instead of routing to a skill. **The two files are not meant to be identical — do not "fix" the difference by symlinking them.**

# Shell / Environment (Windows)

- This is the Baylor-managed Windows laptop. Native shell is PowerShell 7 (`pwsh`) / Windows PowerShell; Claude Code hooks run under Git Bash, where `$HOME` is `/c/Users/eric_rash`.
- Prefer Desktop Commander over Windows-MCP when both could do the job.
- Tool paths: `~/.claude/TOOLPATHS.md` is Mac-centric; on this machine verify with `Get-Command <tool>` / `where.exe <tool>`.
- Traps:
  - `uv` lives at `~/.local/bin/uv.exe`. Hooks call `$HOME/.local/bin/uv`; do not relocate it.
  - No admin rights by default. Anything needing elevation (Hyper-V, diskpart, services) has to be run by Eric in an elevated PowerShell.
  - Docker Desktop (WSL2) hosts Milvus for memsearch. It must be running for memsearch hooks to work.
  - `dcg` is not installed here; the PreToolUse hook is guarded and passes through.
  - Paths with spaces are common (`G:\My Drive\...`, `OneDrive - Baylor University`). Quote them.
  - Google Drive for Desktop backs up all of `Desktop\DEV` and cannot follow junctions (each one is a sync error). So renv project libraries live outside DEV: user env var `RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY_ROOT` = `%LOCALAPPDATA%\R\renv-library` (set 2026-09-22). Do not undo it; restart RStudio after env changes. `DEV\_DRIVE` and `LibraryProject\ZoteroInjestion` are junctions kept on purpose (2 expected Drive errors).
  - R is at `C:\Program Files\R\R-4.5.3\bin\Rscript.exe` (not on PATH).
- DEV projects live at `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV` (one root, one repo per project; Football/ sub-projects are their own repos).
- Primary storage drive (documents, data, deliverables): `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive` (Google Drive; moved off Baylor OneDrive 2026-09-10).
- Legacy tool scripts for the migration live in `C:\DEV\_tools`.

# ~/DEV — workspace map

Eric Rash — Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics. Sport science and
football analytics, plus the agent system that runs them.

This file is a **map, not a rulebook**. Behavior rules live in
`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Read only the index you need.

## Areas

| Area | Index | What lives there |
|---|---|---|
| Football | `FOOTBALL.md` | Game film, player analytics, CFB prediction. ~39k files — about two thirds of DEV. |
| Performance | `PERFORMANCE.md` | Athlete monitoring, testing, load, risk. GPS, force plate, VALD, DEXA, S2. |
| Research | `RESEARCH.md` | Literature, Zotero, book library, reading pipelines. |
| Platform | `PLATFORM.md` | KeystoneOS, dashboards, CLIs, scheduled jobs. |
| Program | `PROGRAM.md` | Staff reporting, curriculum, proposals, vetting, brand. |
| Personal | `PERSONAL.md` | Side projects. Not Baylor work. |
| Commands | `COMMANDS.md` | Desk reference: every report/project command Eric can run himself. |

## Elsewhere on disk

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `~/DEV/_ARCHIVE/` | Parked projects. Not a git repo, so the consolidation sweep skips it. Has its own `README.md`. |
| `~/DEV/_INBOX/` | Loose files from the `~/DEV` root. Own repo. |
| `~/SecondBrain/` | Obsidian vault, ~850 notes. Own `CLAUDE.md`. |
| `~/.claude/skills/` | ~155 skills |
| `~/go/bin/` | 8 custom CLIs built with `cli-printing-press` |
| `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/knowledge/` | ~230 compiled articles |

## Layout rules

Full rules — grouping depth, the depth-2 discovery limit, and the gitignored-subtree
trap — live in project memory: `project_dev-layout-and-discovery.md`.

- 23 projects carry their own `CLAUDE.md`. Read it before working in one.

## Handling care

- `DexaProject/` holds identifiable health data. It lives on Google Drive, not in
  `~/DEV`, on **both** machines — one copy, reached by each machine's own path:
  - Mac: `~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-eric.rash11@gmail.com/My Drive/00_Primary_Storage_Drive/DexaProject`
  - Windows: `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\DexaProject`

  See `PERFORMANCE.md`.
  Never paste its contents into chat, an artifact, or an external service.

## Keeping this true

When a file moves or a new project starts, **update the router in the same
turn**. A stale pointer is worse than no pointer.

The counts above are approximate on purpose — they convey scale, not state, and
a `~` keeps ordinary growth from making this file wrong. Re-measure them only
when one is off by enough to change a decision. Counts last checked 2026-09-05.

Memory files named in these indexes (`project_*.md`, `user_*.md`) live at
`~/.claude/projects/-Users-kristinarash-DEV/memory/`. They auto-load only when
cwd is `~/DEV` itself — from inside a sub-project, open them by path.

Search everything with `memsearch search "<query>" --top-k 5`.

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.

# Synthesis note template

One note per practical question, drafted in `docs/synthesis/`, reviewed by Eric, then promoted to
the vault and linked from the domain advisor. A note is finished when Eric has answered its open
questions, not when it is written. Length: 2 to 3 pages.

## Voices (same rules as the library)
- Source claims are plain text with a `[[library-entry]]` link and the entry's confidence in brackets, e.g. `[supported]`.
- Evidence from Zotero or the web that is not a library entry is labelled **External:** with author, year and page.
- Eric's documented positions (`docs/method-baseline.md`) are labelled **Eric's baseline:**. Positions from the HHPR 5355 transcripts are labelled **Course baseline (HHPR 5355, speaker unconfirmed):** until Eric claims them.
- The writer's own synthesis is labelled **Inference:**.
- No em dashes. Plain, direct sentences.

## Sections
1. **The question**: as asked, and how it actually breaks down. Say plainly when the sources answer a different question from the one being asked.
2. **Bottom line**: 3 to 5 sentences a coach could act on, each tagged with its confidence.
3. **Where the sources agree**: each point with links and confidence.
4. **Where they disagree**: both sides, links, confidence, and what would settle it.
5. **What transfers and what does not**: when the sources come from a different sport or population.
6. **What none of them covers**: gaps, and which uningested chapter or paper would fill each.
7. **Eric's baseline**: the documented positions, labelled as above, and how they sit against sections 3 to 5.
8. **Questions for Eric**: 4 to 6 numbered questions whose answers would settle the note.
9. **Sources used**: library entries (with confidence) and external papers.

1	---
2	type: evidence-map
3	topic: peaking and tapering for collegiate (in-season) American football
4	status: working draft, input to the first Flint synthesis note
5	built: 2026-09-27
6	source-scope: SecondBrain/Knowledge/library reviewed entries only; no PDFs re-opened
7	---
8	
9	# Evidence map: peaking and tapering for collegiate American football
10	
11	## How to read this
12	
13	- Every item gives: the claim in the source's own voice, the entry link, the entry's
14	  `confidence:`, the locator the entry already gives, and a transfer verdict for a
15	  weekly-game college football season (yes / partly / no) with an "Inference:" line.
16	- The claim line is the source's statement only. Football mappings that the library
17	  entries themselves add (bowl prep, bye weeks, Saturday shifts) are the entry writer's
18	  Inference, not the source author's, and appear here only in Inference lines.
19	- Research-paper entries are paper briefs with no `confidence:` field. They are marked
20	  "n/a (paper brief)". Do not read that as low or high confidence.
21	- Bompa (`periodization--bompa`) Ch 1-2 entries carry a chapter locator only (Ch 1 =
22	  printed pp. 3-30, Ch 2 = printed pp. 31-56). No page is given inside the entries.
23	- Evans entries are lecture slides (Unit/Lesson/slide page) and all `untested`. Several
24	  cite Bompa or Issurin secondhand with no edition or page.
25	- Issurin (2008) locators are the 0-based PDF index (printed + 11), as the entries use.
26	- Framing: every peaking model in the library was built on single-event or discrete-meet
27	  sports (swimmers, kayakers, throwers, track). Football has 12+ weekly games and no single
28	  peak, so "transfers" below usually means the direction or the structure transfers, not
29	  the numbers.
30	
31	## Top 5 transferable findings (for the synthesis writer)
32	
33	1. C1: Issurin's in-season two-mini-block week is the only structure in the library that
34	   names American football (strength early week, key practice late week, 28-30 h between).
35	2. B8: strength holds near pre-season for 14-16 weeks of season, then drops sharply (Fleck
36	   & Kraemer via Issurin), the only in-season detraining figure in the library.
37	3. A6 with B11: in the days before competition cut volume, keep frequency, raise the share of
38	   max-speed and sport-specific work; keep strength exercises at lower volume for maintenance.
39	4. F2 with E4: after training, RSImod and flight-time-to-contraction-time stay depressed at
40	   24-72 h while jump height recovers, so strategy metrics are the better game-week read.
41	5. D13 with D14: fast-force qualities and sprint stay impaired 72-96 h after a match, which
42	   sets a floor on how early in the week high-intensity work can return.
43	
44	---
45	
46	## A. Taper and realization prescriptions
47	
48	**A1.** The realization mesocycle (the taper) lasts one to three weeks depending on
49	competition importance, with workload "much lower than in preceding mesocycles," aimed at
50	peak performance, full restoration, maximal speed, event tactics, and readiness.
51	[[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]] ·
52	supported · PDF pp. 122-123 (printed 111-112), Table 3.12 · **Transfers: partly.**
53	Inference: only football windows with 1-3 game-free weeks fit (bowl prep, the last camp week
54	before the opener); a normal game week has no room for a multi-week taper.
55	
56	**A2.** Taper duration is "extremely important and sensitive": too long risks detraining,
57	too short may not restore; a short realization mesocycle demands a fast workload decrease,
58	a longer one allows a gradual one (Mujika et al., 2004). Same entry · supported ·
59	PDF p. 123 (printed 112) · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: this is the core logic for a
60	long bowl gap (see B4); inside a 7-day week the "fast decrease" is already how Thursday to
61	Saturday works.
62	
63	**A3.** A worked two-week kayak realization dosage: 4-6 quasi-competitive races, 8-12
64	broken race simulations, 10-16 start-quarter simulations, 8-12 mid-race simulations, 3-5
65	warm-up rehearsals. Same entry · supported · PDF p. 124 (printed 113), Table 3.13 ·
66	**Transfers: no.** Inference: a football game cannot be rehearsed at full competitive
67	intensity like a race segment; only the idea of segment rehearsal (situational packages)
68	carries.
69	
70	**A4.** Workload reduction during a taper markedly improves mood, mainly through better
71	recovery (Mujika et al., 2004); moderate pre-competition anxiety helps, excessive anxiety
72	hurts, and elite athletes benefit more from raised anxiety than sub-elite (Raglin & Wilson,
73	2000). Same entry · supported · PDF p. 124 (printed 113), section 3.2.3 · **Transfers:
74	partly.** Inference: relevant to bowl games and rivalry weeks; the anxiety-by-level claim is
75	stated without its population in the entry.
76	
77	**A5.** During a two-week taper energy expenditure fell while intake stayed flat; body mass
78	did not change but fat mass rose 4.3%, so body mass alone is not a reliable taper marker
79	(Margaritis et al., 2003). Same entry · supported · PDF pp. 126-127 (printed 115-116); the
80	entry records a source inconsistency ("by up to 69.3%" in text vs about 69% of baseline in
81	Fig 3.10) and that the primary abstract shows n = 16, not 20 · **Transfers: yes.**
82	Inference: any low-load football window (bye week, bowl gap, post-season) invites the same
83	drift, and linemen with high intake are the group most exposed.
84	
85	**A6.** The pre-competitive (tuning) microcycle cuts total volume and the volume of intense
86	exercise substantially, raises the share of maximal-speed/power and sport-specific tasks,
87	usually keeps workout frequency similar, and increases restorative work.
88	[[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] · supported ·
89	PDF p. 105 (printed 94), Table 3.5 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: this is the direction a
90	football game week already follows from midweek to game day, and the template for the final
91	bowl-prep and opener weeks. Eric's review (baseline, via the entry): "maintain intensity,
92	reduce volume" agrees in direction.
93	
94	**A7.** Frequency is kept because extra free time "can be a serious disadvantage"; in
95	qualified athletes at a pre-competitive camp that means eight to ten workouts per week.
96	Same entry · supported · PDF p. 106 (printed 95) · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: the
97	principle (hold the routine, shrink each session) fits football; the 8-10 count is an
98	individual-sport camp figure and should not be read as a session target.
99	
100	**A8.** Peak-effort sessions should be scheduled at the competition's time of day (Olympic
101	regattas run in the morning, so pre-Olympic key sessions are morning sessions). Same entry ·
102	supported · PDF p. 107 (printed 96) · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: kickoff time varies week
103	to week (noon vs night games); the entry base gives no football data on this.
104	
105	**A9.** High-resistance work before competition is disputed: swimmers, volleyball and tennis
106	players report it degrades fine technique (Platonov & Fesenko, 1990), while sport-specific
107	strength work is argued to maintain the force component (Bompa & Carrera, 2003) and, uncited,
108	to prevent stress-hormone muscle loss. Same entry · supported · PDF p. 108 (printed 97) ·
109	**Transfers: partly.** Inference: this is the "do we lift heavy in bowl week / game week"
110	question, and the source presents both sides as live. See Disagreements D-5.
111	
112	**A10.** Research built on the fitness-fatigue model suggests accepted taper protocols "may
113	be too rigorous and short" (Fitz-Clarke et al., 1991), that placement of volume in the taper
114	is a key factor, and that high volume in the days just before competition may be
115	detrimental (Shepley 1992; Zarkadas 1995; Mujika 1996).
116	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] ·
117	supported · PDF pp. 99-100 (printed 88-89) · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: "no high
118	volume in the last days" transfers to Thursday to Saturday; the duration findings come from
119	1990s endurance studies.
120	
121	**A11.** Some Russian restoration specialists deliberately avoid restoring every muscle group
122	after every session, because supercompensation is reportedly more pronounced after partial
123	than total restoration. Same entry · supported · PDF pp. 99-100 (printed 88-89) ·
124	**Transfers: partly.** Inference: may apply to early-week training days; it runs against the
125	football goal of full readiness on game day and has no team-sport data.
126	
127	**A12.** In adolescent futsal players, CMJ-regulated intensification followed by a two-week
128	stepped taper raised CMJ above baseline (ES 0.30), while a preplanned group did not change
129	significantly. [[research-papers/claudino-2016-autoregulating-jump-performance-to-induce-functional-overreaching]]
130	· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 2, 4 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: a model for the camp-to-
131	opener sequence (intensify, then taper, jump-guided); n = 9 per group, U17 futsal.
132	
133	**A13.** In professional rugby union, planned download weeks typically carried 70-80% of the
134	load of the other weeks in the block (authors' applied observation).
135	[[research-papers/comyns-2013-applications-of-the-session-rating-of-perceived-exertion-system-in-professional-rugby-unio]]
136	· n/a (paper brief) · p. 6 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: the only numeric download
137	anchor from a collision team sport in the library; experience-based, no outcomes reported.

511	responds to load, CMJ height alone may be insensitive, HR measures are context-dependent, and
512	MDC is not the same as a practical anchor.
513	[[research-papers/thorpe-2017-monitoring-fatigue-status-in-elite-team-sport-athletes-implications-for-practice]]
514	· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 2-5 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: matches the football CMJ
515	findings in F2 and E4.
516	
517	**E4.** At 72 h after intermittent running, flight time changed only -0.7% while
518	flight-time-to-contraction-time fell 7.7% and total duration rose 7.6%.
519	[[research-papers/gathercole-2015-alternative-countermovement-jump-analysis-to-quantify-acute-neuromuscular-fatigue]]
520	· n/a (paper brief) · p. 7 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: strategy variables catch fatigue
521	that jump height hides; n = 8 college team-sport athletes.
522	
523	**E5.** No-arm-swing CMJ is better for acute readiness, arm-swing for longer-term change;
524	several phase-duration and RFD variables failed reliability thresholds.
525	[[research-papers/heishman-2020-countermovement-jump-reliability-performed-with-and-without-an-arm-swing-in-ncaa-division]]
526	· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 5-12 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: D1 basketball, not
527	football; protocol choice still applies.
528	
529	**E6.** No definitive diagnostic tool for overtraining syndrome exists; rely on sound training
530	theory plus performance monitoring.
531	[[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]]
532	· untested · U3 L2 p. 17 · **Transfers: yes.**
533	
534	**E7.** The overtraining continuum: acute fatigue (days), functional overreaching (days to
535	weeks, temporary decrease), non-functional overreaching (weeks to months), overtraining
536	(months to a year). [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]]
537	· untested · U3 L1 p. 10 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: NFOR mid-season costs games, so
538	the in-season target is to stay at acute fatigue or brief FOR.
539	
540	**E8.** Overwork splits into sympathetic and parasympathetic forms, illustrated with an
541	Omegawave HRV case. [[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--sympathetic-vs-parasympathetic-overtraining-and-omegawave-readiness-case]]
542	· untested · U3 L1 pp. 15-18 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: the symptom tables carry no
543	named source.
544	
545	**E9.** "Monitoring is a compass, not a GPS unit"; start simple, be consistent.
546	[[elite-sports-performance--evans/heuristic--monitoring-is-a-compass-not-a-gps]] · untested ·
547	U4 L1 p. 23 · **Transfers: yes.**
548	
549	**E10.** Monitoring ("has something changed now," days to weeks) and testing ("did capacity
550	improve across a phase," weeks to months) are different questions needing different analysis.
551	[[old-bull-performance-course--old-bull/framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] · supported ·
552	Lab 2C pp. 1-2 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: in-season readiness is monitoring; whether the
553	season kept camp gains is testing.
554	
555	**E11.** System reliability (ICC, SEM, MDC95) and individual sensitivity (within-athlete CV,
556	SWC) are separate questions a decision gate depends on.
557	[[old-bull-performance-course--old-bull/framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] ·
558	supported · Lab 2E p. 1 · **Transfers: yes.**
559	
560	**E12.** When a metric is noisy, widen the threshold, tighten the protocol, or choose a more
561	stable metric for decision gates.
562	[[old-bull-performance-course--old-bull/heuristic--fix-protocol-before-trusting-a-noisy-metric]]
563	· supported · Lab 2E p. 2 · **Transfers: yes.**
564	
565	**E13.** Honest questionnaire answers depend on trust, explained purpose, visible use and
566	low burden; athletes conceal when they fear staff reaction or selection impact.
567	[[research-papers/mccall-2023-a-qualitative-study-of-11-world-class-team-sport-athletes-experiences-answering-subjective]]
568	· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 9-11 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: sample includes American
569	football players; explains the gamed-survey history in E2.
570	
571	**E14.** Monitor at least one actionable variable per quadrant: metabolic load, neuromuscular
572	load, metabolic response, neuromuscular response.
573	[[research-papers/buchheit-undated-data-everywhere-insight-nowhere-a-practical-quadrant-based-model-for-monitoring-training-l]]
574	· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 3, 10-11 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: expert opinion from
575	soccer; the submaximal-run HR test is hard to schedule in a football week.
576	
577	**E15.** Separate training load, athlete state and training response; readiness is an
578	operational proxy; tools should be "minimal, adequate, and accurate," with individual
579	reference values from standardized repeated testing.
580	[[research-papers/rebelo-2026-monitoring-training-effects-in-athletes-a-multidimensional-framework-for-decision-making]]
581	· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 2-15 · **Transfers: yes.**
582	
583	**E16.** Load data support feedback, in-session adjustment, day-to-day and season planning;
584	no single metric predicts injury.
585	[[research-papers/west-2021-more-than-a-metric-how-training-load-is-used-in-elite-sport-for-athlete-management]]
586	· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 2-4 · **Transfers: yes.**
587	
588	**E17.** ACWR offered no meaningful predictive advantage over an intercept-only model, and
589	contrived denominators reproduced its associations; the defensible rule is only "not too much
590	too soon." [[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor]]
591	(p. 4-5) and [[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-training-load-and-injury-part-2-questionable-research-practices-hijack-the-truth-and-misle]]
592	(p. 1) · n/a (paper briefs) · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: do not build in-season taper
593	triggers on ACWR. Griffin 2020
594	([[research-papers/griffin-2020-the-association-between-the-acute-chronic-workload-ratio-and-injury-and-its-application-in]],
595	p. 1) reports associations but only within multifactorial monitoring.
596	
597	**E18.** Impaired hamstring strength beyond about 48 h post-match was used as a secondary-
598	prevention signal, with one injury vs five in a historical control.
599	[[research-papers/wollin-2020-a-novel-hamstring-strain-injury-prevention-system-post-match-strength-testing-for-secondar]]
600	· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 1-2 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: a candidate midweek check
601	in football; U17 soccer, non-randomized.
602	
603	## F. Specific to American football
604	
605	**F1.** In one D1 program (39 players, 15-week season), starters with higher
606	testosterone-to-cortisol ratios had lower soreness and better sleep, while nonstarters showed
607	poorer recovery with higher IL-6/cortisol despite lower external load; exploratory, not NFOR
608	diagnosis. [[research-papers/aychman-2026-multimodal-indicators-of-non-functional-overreaching-in-ncaa-division-i-american-football]]
609	· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 1, 9 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: the only in-season
610	overreaching study in football in the library; argues for separate readiness reads for
611	starters and developmental players.
612	
613	**F2.** In D1 football, jump height, mean power and peak velocity recovered to small
614	reductions by 24 h after training, while flight-time-to-contraction-time and RSImod stayed
615	largely reduced at 24 h; athletes preserved output by changing strategy.
616	[[research-papers/lewis-undated-athlete-monitoring-in-american-collegiate-football]] · n/a
617	(paper brief) · pp. 96-97 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: supports RSImod as the game-week
618	readiness marker over jump height; n = 5 per CMJ study.
619	
620	**F3.** Across 10 seasons in one D1 program, total load rose with snap count but per-snap load
621	fell; offensive total load related positively to PFF grade, while higher per-snap intensity on
622	defense related to lower grades (associations only).
623	[[research-papers/lever-2026-game-exposure-shapes-intensity-and-performance-in-division-i-college-football]]
624	· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 5-7, 10 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: game load differs by
625	exposure group and position, so the "game" in a game-week plan is not one dose.
626	
627	**F4.** D1 football players in one sample slept about 6.3 h per night, and nights with naps
628	had about 18 fewer minutes of sleep.
629	[[research-papers/lever-2024-a-preliminary-investigation-of-the-relationship-between-sleep-and-nap-behavior-of-ncaa-div]]
630	· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 4-5 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: sleep is a live readiness
631	limiter in season; n = 3 athletes.
632	
633	**F5.** In D1-A televised games, plays averaged 5.2 s with about 36 s rest between plays
634	(excluding long stoppages), an exercise-to-rest ratio near 1:7.
635	[[research-papers/iosia-2008-analysis-of-exercise-to-rest-ratios-during-division-ia-televised-football-competition]]
636	· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 3-4, 7 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: defines the conditioning
637	quality to maintain in season; 2004 data, before modern tempo offenses.
638	
639	**F6.** CMJ profiles differ by position group (linemen, hybrids, skill, specialists); four
640	components explain 89.5% of force-time variance, so monitor one or two nonredundant metrics
641	from each. [[research-papers/merrigan-2022-comparisons-of-countermovement-jump-force-time-characteristics-among-national-collegiate-a]]
642	· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 1-5 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: readiness thresholds should be
643	position-specific; off-season data only.
644	
645	**F7.** A ten-step annual-plan process worked through for an American football wide receiver:
646	profile, calendar, periodization model, phases (including Unloading/Tapering), bioenergetic,
647	biodynamic and biomotor sequences, meso/microcycles, workouts, assessment and monitoring.
648	[[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]] ·
649	untested · U3 L7 pp. 2-13 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: a planning checklist that names
650	football, but it does not say which cycle model the WR example uses and gives no taper
651	content.
652	
653	Cross-listed football items counted elsewhere: C1 (Issurin in-season week names American
654	football), B8 (Fleck & Kraemer 14-16 weeks), B17 (Stokes names American football),
655	E13 (McCall sample includes American football).
656	
657	Not evidence: `research-papers/fullagar-2017-updated-review-of-the-applied-physiology-of-american-college-football...`
658	is a retrieval stub with no full text ("a retrieval lead rather than reviewed evidence").
659	`de-souza-2023-iron-deficiencies-following-pre-season-training...` is also a stub.
660	
661	---
662	
663	## Disagreements between sources
664	
665	**D-1. Supercompensation vs adaptive reconstruction.**
666	Side 1: Bompa's supercompensation cycle with fixed windows (36-72 h rebound, 3-7 day
667	involution) [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] (supported, Ch 1), and
668	Issurin's taper and tuning mechanism, "reduced total load is the principal condition for
669	reaching supercompensation" [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]]
670	(supported, PDF p. 106).
671	Side 2: Verkhoshansky and Siff: adaptation is structural and processing change; ATP never
672	depletes significantly, no overshoot is seen beyond glycogen, so load timing "remains
673	indeterminate" [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]
674	(contested, PDF pp. 94-99). Bompa's own entry concedes modern sport science prefers the
675	two-factor model. The Verkhoshansky text also contradicts itself (printed 85 vs 88).
676	
677	**D-2. Is the fitness-fatigue model usable for timing a peak?**
678	Side 1: Evans: "JUST A CONCEPT," no empirical evidence for a multi-quality model, no
679	citation [[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept]]
680	(untested, U1 L5 pp. 3-4).
681	Side 2: Bompa's 3:1 fatigue-to-fitness decay rule [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]
682	(supported, Ch 1), and Verkhoshansky's formal Banister model plus the taper-timing studies
683	built on it [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]]
684	(supported, PDF pp. 99-100).
685	Inference: the two are closer than they look. Evans objects to one model covering all
686	qualities; the Verkhoshansky entry says the constants must be fit per athlete and per phase.
687	Afonso 2019 (D16) sides with the caution: no study tested predicted peak timing.
688	
689	**D-3. Issurin 2008 vs Issurin 2016 on lower-level athletes.**
690	Side 1: the 2008 book says the traditional mixed model "has visible benefits" for low- and
691	mid-level athletes and medium concentration is enough for them
692	[[block-periodization--issurin/principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (contested,
693	PDF p. 44, printed 33).
694	Side 2: the 2016 review says there is "no evidence that amateur athletes have any serious
695	restrictions" with highly concentrated block workloads
696	[[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]
697	(n/a, p. 11). Per the brief's last Key-findings bullet, the 2016 critique of the
698	concentrated-unidirectional model (pp. 6-7) targets Verkhoshansky's model, not the book's
699	A-T-R model, so that part is not a contradiction.
700	
701	**D-4. Taper aggressiveness.**
702	Side 1: Issurin: a short realization mesocycle "demands a fast workload decrease"
703	[[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]]
704	(supported, PDF p. 123).
705	Side 2: Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991): accepted tapers "may be too rigorous and short"
706	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]]
707	(supported, printed 88-89). The Issurin entry flags this tension itself and neither text
708	resolves it.
709	
710	**D-5. Heavy strength work in the taper.**
711	Side 1: reduce or exclude it (swimmers, volleyball, tennis; Platonov & Fesenko, 1990).
712	Side 2: keep sport-specific maximal/explosive strength to hold the force component (Bompa &
713	Carrera, 2003) and, uncited, to prevent hormone-driven muscle loss. Both in
714	[[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] (supported,
715	PDF p. 108). Bondarchuk's maintain-at-lower-volume rule (B11, supported) leans toward side 2.
716	
717	**D-6. Residual durations and the order of detraining.**
718	Side 1: Issurin Table 1.6: aerobic and max strength retained longest (30 ± 5 days), max speed
719	shortest (5 ± 3) [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]
720	(contested, PDF p. 35).
721	Side 2: Eric's own course material (class-4-2026.md p. 47 via method-baseline): aerobic traits
722	are lost fastest and alactic/speed slowest; the class-1 transcript frames 30-day windows as
723	conditional on a small retention dose. The entry says do not harmonize: this may be residual
724	after cessation vs loss rate without a retention dose. Carry forward as is and resolve with
725	Eric.
726	
727	**D-7. In-season emphasis: max strength vs ballistic work.**
728	Side 1: Issurin's in-season week prioritizes maximal strength to protect anabolic status.
729	Side 2: Newton et al. (2006) sequenced heavy resistance with ballistic microcycles to improve
730	jumping. Both in [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]]
731	(supported, PDF pp. 109-110).
732	
733	**D-8. Transmutation monitoring: subjective vs objective markers.**
734	Side 1: the book's retelling of Hooper et al. (1995): only subjective ratings separated stale
735	swimmers, and a larger objective battery did not improve prediction.
736	Side 2: the entry's primary-abstract check: n = 14 not 19, staleness partly defined from
737	fatigue ratings (circular), and resting catecholamines plus stress ratings explained 85% vs
738	76% for subjective ratings alone. Both in
739	[[block-periodization--issurin/framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]
740	(supported, PDF p. 121). A third, practical side: Eric's baseline records the daily wellness
741	survey was gamed at roster scale and dropped; McCall 2023 (E13) frames honest answering as a
742	trust problem.
743	
744	**D-9. Does the periodization literature support peaking at all?**
745	Side 1: Evans: "classic" (Soviet/Eastern) literature supports multidimensional planned
746	periodization with long-term elite studies
747	[[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--periodization-evidence-classic-vs-nonclassic-literature-debate]]
748	(untested, U3 L4 pp. 13-14).
749	Side 2: Afonso 2019: no study in the meta-analyses isolated periodization or tested predicted
750	peak timing (D16); Harries 2015: linear and undulating give equal strength gains (D17).
751	
752	---
753	
754	## Gaps: football peaking questions no entry answers
755	
756	Items where the library has only the entry writer's Inference count as gaps.
757	
758	1. **Bye weeks.** No source addresses a mid-season bye. The mini-block top-up idea (B4, B7) is
759	   the entry writer's mapping, and step loading's unloading week (C9) is not tied to a season.
760	2. **Short weeks and Thursday or Friday games.** Galiano (C7) is soccer and descriptive;
761	   Issurin's in-season week assumes a 7-day cycle and a Sunday game.
762	3. **Fall camp to week 1.** No source covers the camp-to-opener transition. The transmutation
763	   cap (B9) and pre-competitive week (A6) are mapped to camp only by Inference; Claudino (A12)
764	   is U17 futsal.
765	4. **Postseason and the bowl gap.** The whole bowl-prep structure (A1, B4, B10) is Inference
766	   from kayak and pre-Olympic calendars. Nothing covers a conference championship followed by
767	   an uncertain bowl date, or the playoff format with consecutive high-stakes games.
768	5. **Position-group differences in peaking.** Merrigan (F6) is an off-season CMJ profile,
769	   Aychman (F1) is starter vs nonstarter, Lever 2026 (F3) is game load by exposure. None says
770	   how taper or maintenance dose should differ for linemen vs skill players.
771	6. **Any football taper dose-response.** No entry reports a taper or unloading trial in
772	   American football.
773	7. **Detraining across a football season.** The only figure is Fleck & Kraemer's 14-16 weeks,
774	   secondhand via Issurin (B8). No in-season strength or speed retention data from football.
775	8. **Starters vs non-playing players in season.** Aychman hints they differ; no source
776	   prescribes make-up conditioning or loading for low-snap players.
777	9. **Travel, academic calendar, NCAA practice-hour limits.** Named as constraints by entry
778	   writers; no source addresses them.
779	10. **Game time of day.** Issurin's time-of-day rule (A8) has no football or night-game data.
780	11. **How long sports form lasts once reached, and whether a team can hold it for 12+ weeks.**
781	    Bondarchuk (D11) gives time to enter form, not time held.
782	
783	### Uningested chapters and sources that would help
784	
785	- **Bompa Ch 7 "Peaking for Competition"** (printed 187-202, PDF 198-213): the named gap in
786	  the 2026-09-03 miss-log line. Also Ch 5 "Rest and Recovery" (printed 97-124), Ch 6 "Annual
787	  Training Plan" (125-186), Ch 8 "Training Cycles" (203-234). All pending.
788	- **Issurin Ch 4 "Long-term preparation"** (printed 125-159, PDF 136-170): annual and
789	  multi-year cycles. **Ch 5 "Altitude training"** (printed 160-201): low priority for
790	  football per the ingest map.
791	- **Verkhoshansky Ch 4-9** pending; Supertraining's later chapters include periodization and
792	  restoration material not yet in the library.
793	- **Bondarchuk Vol I Ch 3** pending.
794	- **Fullagar et al. 2017** (applied physiology of American college football): stub only, full
795	  text needed.
796	- Evans's Bompa-cited entries (C12, A14) should be checked against Bompa Ch 6-7 once ingested,
797	  since they carry no edition or page.
798	
799	---
800	
801	## Library hygiene notes found while mapping
802	
803	- Two Issurin entries
804	  ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]]
805	  and [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]])
806	  quote "Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review states" that block-periodization evidence
807	  "does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American
808	  football." In the Issurin 2016 paper brief, that sentence is an unlocated bullet under
809	  "Limitations and applicability," written by the brief writer, not a quote from Issurin.
810	  It should be relabeled as the brief's assessment (Inference) in both entries.
811	- Research-paper briefs have no `confidence:` field, so the synthesis note cannot rank them
812	  on the same scale as book entries.
813	- Bompa Ch 1-2 entries give chapter locators only; a reviewer cannot check them to the page.
