---
type: evidence-map
topic: peaking and tapering for collegiate (in-season) American football
status: working draft, input to the first Flint synthesis note
built: 2026-09-27
source-scope: SecondBrain/Knowledge/library reviewed entries only; no PDFs re-opened
---

# Evidence map: peaking and tapering for collegiate American football

## How to read this

- Every item gives: the claim in the source's own voice, the entry link, the entry's
  `confidence:`, the locator the entry already gives, and a transfer verdict for a
  weekly-game college football season (yes / partly / no) with an "Inference:" line.
- The claim line is the source's statement only. Football mappings that the library
  entries themselves add (bowl prep, bye weeks, Saturday shifts) are the entry writer's
  Inference, not the source author's, and appear here only in Inference lines.
- Research-paper entries are paper briefs with no `confidence:` field. They are marked
  "n/a (paper brief)". Do not read that as low or high confidence.
- Bompa (`periodization--bompa`) Ch 1-2 entries carry a chapter locator only (Ch 1 =
  printed pp. 3-30, Ch 2 = printed pp. 31-56). No page is given inside the entries.
- Evans entries are lecture slides (Unit/Lesson/slide page) and all `untested`. Several
  cite Bompa or Issurin secondhand with no edition or page.
- Issurin (2008) locators are the 0-based PDF index (printed + 11), as the entries use.
- Framing: every peaking model in the library was built on single-event or discrete-meet
  sports (swimmers, kayakers, throwers, track). Football has 12+ weekly games and no single
  peak, so "transfers" below usually means the direction or the structure transfers, not
  the numbers.

## Top 5 transferable findings (for the synthesis writer)

1. C1: Issurin's in-season two-mini-block week is the only structure in the library that
   names American football (strength early week, key practice late week, 28-30 h between).
2. B8: strength holds near pre-season for 14-16 weeks of season, then drops sharply (Fleck
   & Kraemer via Issurin), the only in-season detraining figure in the library.
3. A6 with B11: in the days before competition cut volume, keep frequency, raise the share of
   max-speed and sport-specific work; keep strength exercises at lower volume for maintenance.
4. F2 with E4: after training, RSImod and flight-time-to-contraction-time stay depressed at
   24-72 h while jump height recovers, so strategy metrics are the better game-week read.
5. D13 with D14: fast-force qualities and sprint stay impaired 72-96 h after a match, which
   sets a floor on how early in the week high-intensity work can return.

---

## A. Taper and realization prescriptions

**A1.** The realization mesocycle (the taper) lasts one to three weeks depending on
competition importance, with workload "much lower than in preceding mesocycles," aimed at
peak performance, full restoration, maximal speed, event tactics, and readiness.
[[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]] ·
supported · PDF pp. 122-123 (printed 111-112), Table 3.12 · **Transfers: partly.**
Inference: only football windows with 1-3 game-free weeks fit (bowl prep, the last camp week
before the opener); a normal game week has no room for a multi-week taper.

**A2.** Taper duration is "extremely important and sensitive": too long risks detraining,
too short may not restore; a short realization mesocycle demands a fast workload decrease,
a longer one allows a gradual one (Mujika et al., 2004). Same entry · supported ·
PDF p. 123 (printed 112) · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: this is the core logic for a
long bowl gap (see B4); inside a 7-day week the "fast decrease" is already how Thursday to
Saturday works.

**A3.** A worked two-week kayak realization dosage: 4-6 quasi-competitive races, 8-12
broken race simulations, 10-16 start-quarter simulations, 8-12 mid-race simulations, 3-5
warm-up rehearsals. Same entry · supported · PDF p. 124 (printed 113), Table 3.13 ·
**Transfers: no.** Inference: a football game cannot be rehearsed at full competitive
intensity like a race segment; only the idea of segment rehearsal (situational packages)
carries.

**A4.** Workload reduction during a taper markedly improves mood, mainly through better
recovery (Mujika et al., 2004); moderate pre-competition anxiety helps, excessive anxiety
hurts, and elite athletes benefit more from raised anxiety than sub-elite (Raglin & Wilson,
2000). Same entry · supported · PDF p. 124 (printed 113), section 3.2.3 · **Transfers:
partly.** Inference: relevant to bowl games and rivalry weeks; the anxiety-by-level claim is
stated without its population in the entry.

**A5.** During a two-week taper energy expenditure fell while intake stayed flat; body mass
did not change but fat mass rose 4.3%, so body mass alone is not a reliable taper marker
(Margaritis et al., 2003). Same entry · supported · PDF pp. 126-127 (printed 115-116); the
entry records a source inconsistency ("by up to 69.3%" in text vs about 69% of baseline in
Fig 3.10) and that the primary abstract shows n = 16, not 20 · **Transfers: yes.**
Inference: any low-load football window (bye week, bowl gap, post-season) invites the same
drift, and linemen with high intake are the group most exposed.

**A6.** The pre-competitive (tuning) microcycle cuts total volume and the volume of intense
exercise substantially, raises the share of maximal-speed/power and sport-specific tasks,
usually keeps workout frequency similar, and increases restorative work.
[[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] · supported ·
PDF p. 105 (printed 94), Table 3.5 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: this is the direction a
football game week already follows from midweek to game day, and the template for the final
bowl-prep and opener weeks. Eric's review (baseline, via the entry): "maintain intensity,
reduce volume" agrees in direction.

**A7.** Frequency is kept because extra free time "can be a serious disadvantage"; in
qualified athletes at a pre-competitive camp that means eight to ten workouts per week.
Same entry · supported · PDF p. 106 (printed 95) · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: the
principle (hold the routine, shrink each session) fits football; the 8-10 count is an
individual-sport camp figure and should not be read as a session target.

**A8.** Peak-effort sessions should be scheduled at the competition's time of day (Olympic
regattas run in the morning, so pre-Olympic key sessions are morning sessions). Same entry ·
supported · PDF p. 107 (printed 96) · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: kickoff time varies week
to week (noon vs night games); the entry base gives no football data on this.

**A9.** High-resistance work before competition is disputed: swimmers, volleyball and tennis
players report it degrades fine technique (Platonov & Fesenko, 1990), while sport-specific
strength work is argued to maintain the force component (Bompa & Carrera, 2003) and, uncited,
to prevent stress-hormone muscle loss. Same entry · supported · PDF p. 108 (printed 97) ·
**Transfers: partly.** Inference: this is the "do we lift heavy in bowl week / game week"
question, and the source presents both sides as live. See Disagreements D-5.

**A10.** Research built on the fitness-fatigue model suggests accepted taper protocols "may
be too rigorous and short" (Fitz-Clarke et al., 1991), that placement of volume in the taper
is a key factor, and that high volume in the days just before competition may be
detrimental (Shepley 1992; Zarkadas 1995; Mujika 1996).
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] ·
supported · PDF pp. 99-100 (printed 88-89) · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: "no high
volume in the last days" transfers to Thursday to Saturday; the duration findings come from
1990s endurance studies.

**A11.** Some Russian restoration specialists deliberately avoid restoring every muscle group
after every session, because supercompensation is reportedly more pronounced after partial
than total restoration. Same entry · supported · PDF pp. 99-100 (printed 88-89) ·
**Transfers: partly.** Inference: may apply to early-week training days; it runs against the
football goal of full readiness on game day and has no team-sport data.

**A12.** In adolescent futsal players, CMJ-regulated intensification followed by a two-week
stepped taper raised CMJ above baseline (ES 0.30), while a preplanned group did not change
significantly. [[research-papers/claudino-2016-autoregulating-jump-performance-to-induce-functional-overreaching]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 2, 4 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: a model for the camp-to-
opener sequence (intensify, then taper, jump-guided); n = 9 per group, U17 futsal.

**A13.** In professional rugby union, planned download weeks typically carried 70-80% of the
load of the other weeks in the block (authors' applied observation).
[[research-papers/comyns-2013-applications-of-the-session-rating-of-perceived-exertion-system-in-professional-rugby-unio]]
· n/a (paper brief) · p. 6 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: the only numeric download
anchor from a collision team sport in the library; experience-based, no outcomes reported.

**A14.** Bompa's macrocycle includes a distinct Unloading/Tapering phase, described as the
best way to elevate the athlete's preparedness before competition (Evans citing Bompa, 2009).
[[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--bompa-macrocycle-phase-objectives]] · untested ·
U3 L5 pp. 15-19 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: secondhand, no edition or page; the real
taper content is in the uningested Bompa Ch 7.

## B. Residual training effects, maintenance, mini-blocks, retention and detraining

**B1.** Residual training effects after training stops: aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days,
maximum strength 30 ± 5, anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4, strength endurance 15 ± 5,
maximum (alactic) speed 5 ± 3 (Issurin & Lustig, 2004).
[[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]] ·
**contested** · PDF p. 35 (printed 24), Table 1.6 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: the
5-day speed figure is the strongest library argument for max-velocity exposure every game
week; the table is contested against Eric's own course material (see Disagreements D-6), and
the sample behind it is not reported.

**B2.** Aerobic ability and max strength are retained for weeks because they rest on large
morphological and biochemical change; max speed rests on "very delicate and highly precise
neuro-muscular interactions" that cannot be held at the highest level "without specially
organized training." Same entry · contested · PDF pp. 35-36 (printed 24-25) · **Transfers:
yes.** Inference: the mechanism, not the day count, is what justifies protecting speed work
inside the week.

**B3.** Residual thinking has limits: VO2max falls when weekly volume drops below a level
(Steinacker 1993, 1998), and large volumes of intense work do not prevent aerobic detraining
during a taper (Mujika, 1999). Same entry · contested · PDF p. 34 (printed 23) ·
**Transfers: partly.** Inference: warns against assuming the camp aerobic base survives a
low-volume season by default.

**B4.** When a training stage outruns the ~30-day residual, insert a compact mini-block for
the decaying ability rather than adding scattered workouts; a five-week gap between targets
can be run as 10-14 / 10-14 / 8-10 days (accumulation / transmutation / realization) with no
mini-block, while a 7-9 week stage needs longer mesocycles plus a mini-block. Issurin hedges
the remedy ("Apparently") and gives no outcome data.
[[block-periodization--issurin/framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]] ·
supported · PDF pp. 129-131 (printed 118-120), Fig 3.12 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference:
the closest structural answer in the library to the regular-season-to-bowl gap; untested in
any team sport, and bowl dates are not fixed months ahead like a kayak championship.

**B5.** A design based solely on residual lengths "will be extremely rigid and inflexible.
There are also other factors influencing training residuals." Same entry · supported ·
PDF p. 127 (printed 116) · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: the author's own caution against
using B1 as a clock.

**B6.** After Popov competed several times inside an aerobic mesocycle, his anaerobic-
threshold speed lost about half its gain and V-La8 about a quarter within roughly ten days,
attributed to stress hormones and to glycolytic suppression of aerobic enzymes.
[[block-periodization--issurin/case-study--popov-competition-shortens-residual-effects]] ·
untested · PDF pp. 128-129 (printed 117-118), Fig 3.11 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference:
supports expecting a brutal game to erode the base, not just add acute fatigue; one swimmer,
no control, no football test analog.

**B7.** "Prominent coaches" add special aerobic workloads after competition to restore and
revitalize athletes. Same entry · untested · PDF p. 128 (printed 117) · **Transfers: partly.**
Inference: a practice precedent for a light aerobic top-up early in the week after a heavy
game; no dose given.

**B8.** Team-sport players typically keep strength near pre-season levels for 14-16 weeks of
season, after which strength variables decrease dramatically (Fleck & Kraemer, 1997, cited by
Issurin). [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]]
· supported · PDF pp. 108-109 (printed 97-98) · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: a 12-game
season plus conference title game plus bowl runs from camp to roughly week 16-20, right at or
past that edge; this is secondhand and the only in-season detraining figure in the library.

**B9.** The transmutation mesocycle usually lasts no more than four weeks, capped by fatigue
accumulation (3-4 weeks) and by the prior accumulation residual; a 2-4 day aerobic contrast
mini-block can be inserted to prolong aerobic residuals.
[[block-periodization--issurin/framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]
· supported · PDF pp. 118-119 (printed 107-108), Tables 3.9-3.10 · **Transfers: partly.**
Inference: maps to fall camp as the most concentrated block; the cap is Issurin's synthesis
with no dose-response citation.

**B10.** Accumulation gains are steep for about three weeks, reasonable to six, and small
after (kayakers: 1.93%/week, then 0.53%/week, then 0.25-0.13%/week); up to six weeks for deep
change, three weeks or less to refresh, 10-14 days late in the season.
[[block-periodization--issurin/framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]] ·
supported · PDF pp. 113-115 (printed 102-104), Fig 3.9 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference:
the "10-14 day refresh" is the only accumulation length the library offers for a
late-season window such as an early bowl gap; n = 8, unpublished thesis.

**B11.** Specialized-preparatory strength exercises that no longer predict competitive gains
should be kept "to a somewhat lesser volume to maintain the achieved level, as well as for
carrying out restorative measures."
[[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]]
· supported · PDF p. 175 (printed 158) · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: direct support for
in-season maintenance lifting at reduced volume; track and field data.

**B12.** The one method Bondarchuk reports for holding an earlier stage's level is to keep
that stage's exercises in the program at much-reduced volume; he then rejects the
start/middle/end timing model of transfer in favor of transfer over the stage, given
succession.
[[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]]
· untested · PDF pp. 35-37 (printed 18-20) · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: supports carrying
summer and camp exercises into the season at low volume rather than dropping them.

**B13.** Three types of overload: stimulating (above neutral, heightened adaptation),
retaining (neutral zone, maintained preparedness), detraining (performance falls).
[[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--three-types-of-overload-stimulating-retaining-detraining]]
· untested · U2 L4 p. 15 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: useful labels for in-season
intent; no numeric definition of the neutral zone.

**B14.** Biochemical adaptations are gained in a fixed order and lost in reverse; the longer
the training period, the longer the changes persist after training stops (Platonov, 1988).
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] ·
supported · PDF pp. 96-97 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: supports a long, stable summer
base before the season; one secondary source, no timings.

**B15.** Tendons and ligaments strengthen with training and weaken with inactivity; muscle
adapts in days while connective tissue needs weeks to months.
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response]]
(supported, PDF pp. 193-194, printed 182-183) and
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]] (supported,
PDF p. 46, printed 35) · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: argues for continuous high-force
and high-speed exposure through the season and a graded return after a long bowl layoff;
much of the evidence is animal work.

**B16.** A team-sport annual plan can move from eccentric-led off-season work to mostly
isometric in season (pushes, holds, some switches), with plyometrics throughout; Natera
reports eccentric adaptations "stay around" when switches and catches are kept.
[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--eccentric-to-isometric-periodization-team-sport]]
· untested · lesson 16, ~80:44-88:49 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: a low-soreness
in-season maintenance option; one coach's template, and the entry warns it is not a reason to
drop in-season hamstring eccentrics.

**B17.** After prolonged training restriction in collision sports, contact preparation should
progress over at least 3-4 weeks and high-speed running should be reintroduced progressively.
[[research-papers/stokes-2020-returning-to-play-after-prolonged-training-restrictions-in-professional-collision-sports]]
· n/a (paper brief) · p. 7 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: relevant to the summer-to-camp
ramp and to a long bowl layoff, not to weekly peaking; expert opinion, rugby-centered, names
American football as a transfer target.

## C. In-season, multi-competition and team-sport microcycle structure

**C1.** For team sports with a 20-35 week season (soccer, American football, rugby,
volleyball named), split the week into two mini-blocks: early week for sport-specific maximal
and explosive strength (two strength key-workouts), late week for team practice and game prep
(one big key practice, then a load-restricted opponent-specific session before the game),
leaving 28-30 hours between the last strength key-workout and the key practice. Based on
Baker (2001), rugby league. [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]]
· supported · PDF pp. 108-111 (printed 97-100), Fig 3.8 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: the
only library structure that names American football; the worked week assumes a Sunday game
and must shift about one day earlier for Saturday games (entry writer's mapping). Weekly games
"restrict" block sequencing, so Issurin frames this as keeping some benefits, not a
substitute.

**C2.** The in-season chart prioritizes maximal strength over explosive work to protect
"somatic, functional and anabolic status," while noting a counter-example of sequencing heavy
resistance with ballistic microcycles to improve jumping (Newton et al., 2006). Same entry ·
supported · PDF pp. 109-110 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: an open emphasis choice, not
settled. See Disagreements D-7.

**C3.** Build a microcycle from the key-workouts first, then choose the sessions before and
after each deliberately (the one before sets sensitivity to the stimulus, the one after sets
fatigue and restoration), then restorative windows, then supporting work, then monitoring.
[[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--microcycle-construction-key-workout-rules]] ·
supported · PDF pp. 111-112 (printed 100-101), Table 3.6 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: a
usable planning order for a game week; it assumes one dominant modality, which a multi-position
roster does not have.

**C4.** Six microcycle types (adjustment, loading, impact, pre-competitive, competitive,
restoration); the pre-competitive type runs 5-7 days at medium load, tuning with
event-specific means. [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]]
· supported · PDF p. 88 (printed 77), Table 3.1 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: a football
game week is a 7-day pre-competitive-plus-competitive microcycle by this vocabulary; a bye
week can be classed as restoration or loading by choice.

**C5.** Workout load on a 1-5 scale by restoration time (under 12 h to over 72 h), mapped to
Borg RPE bands (6-11 restoration, 12-14 retention, 15-16 substantial, 17-18 large, 19-20
extreme). [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]
· supported · PDF pp. 52-54 (printed 41-43), Tables 2.3-2.4 · **Transfers: partly.**
Inference: a shared vocabulary for labeling each day of a game week; no validation cited.

**C6.** Competition can be inserted inside a transmutation mesocycle; athletes experience the
competitive workload as a relative load reduction and should not expect a personal best.
[[block-periodization--issurin/framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]
· supported · PDF p. 119 (printed 108), Table 3.10 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: the
closest the library comes to "train through" weeks against lesser opponents; no team data.

**C7.** Training-to-match load ratios rise with microcycle length (3 to 6 days: total distance
0.36 to 1.52, high-speed running 0.10 to 0.86); short microcycles give ratios below 1, and
no evidence establishes an optimal ratio.
[[research-papers/galiano-2026-more-matches-less-time-how-load-ratios-reveal-gaps-between-training-and-competition-in-foo]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 4-5 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: speaks to short weeks
(Thursday games) versus normal weeks; soccer, descriptive only.

**C8.** Two schedules with the same weekly load (2,125 AU) produced different strain; the more
homogeneous one raised strain about 30%. Record non-training days as zero load.
[[research-papers/comyns-2013-applications-of-the-session-rating-of-perceived-exertion-system-in-professional-rugby-unio]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 5, 8 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: supports a hard-easy
distribution inside the game week rather than a flat one; experience-based.

**C9.** Step loading: load rises in a wave across three microcycles and drops in a fourth
unloading week (3:1, with 4:2 and 2:1 variants); flat repeated loads create monotony.
[[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]] · proven · Ch 2 ·
**Transfers: partly.** Inference: the weekly game rhythm does not allow a clean 4-week wave;
a bye week is the only calendar-given unloading slot.

**C10.** The annual cycle is built from four to seven training stages of about two months,
each an accumulation-transmutation-realization sequence ending in competition, allowing
multiple peaks. [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]
· supported · PDF pp. 38-40 (printed 27-29) · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: fits the
football off-season (winter, spring, summer, camp) better than the season itself; no
derivation given for stage count.

**C11.** World-class track athletes compete and peak many times per season, not once (Suslov,
2001). [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field]]
· supported · PDF p. 24 (printed 13), Table 1.5 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: the
multi-peak problem generalizes; the evidence is individual sports where "peak" is one
measurable output.

**C12.** Monocycle, bicycle and tricycle annual plans with stated week distributions (Evans
citing Bompa, 2009). [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]]
· untested · U3 L4 pp. 25-30 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: football's calendar is a
monocycle with a very long competitive phase; secondhand, no page.

**C13.** Once a rehab athlete overlaps with team training, the rehab week is shaped around the
team's week (for example a light partial session, full training midweek, and a captain's-run
walkthrough before the match). [[on-field-rtp--harries/framework--fitting-rehab-into-the-team-training-week]]
· untested · Part 6, ~05:18-05:27, ~17:40-18:10, ~38:20 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference:
AFL, n = 3 cases; a model for slotting returning players into the game week, not a template.

**C14.** Track running volume as a percent of game value per metric (HSR, VHSR, sprint), with
the denominator never defined in the course.
[[on-field-rtp--harries/principle--percent-of-game-value-as-volume-metric]] · supported ·
Part 6 throughout; Part 1 ~02:20-02:49 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: a useful way to
dose in-season running by position if Baylor builds position-specific game denominators.

## D. Fitness-fatigue, supercompensation vs adaptive reconstruction, delayed effects, sports form timing

**D1.** Fatigue from a bout dissipates about three times faster than the positive effect
persists (about 24 h vs 72 h); the gain becomes visible only after fatigue clears (Zatsiorsky
and Kraemer, cited by Bompa). [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] ·
supported · Ch 1 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: explains why the heaviest work sits early
in the game week; the entry itself says not to schedule to the hour.

**D2.** Supercompensation cycle: fatigue (1-2 h), compensation (24-48 h), supercompensation
(36-72 h), involution (3-7 days). [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] ·
supported · Ch 1 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: the entry itself notes current sport
science prefers the two-factor model; use as a mental model only.

**D3.** Training effects are immediate, delayed (appearing after fatigue clears, later for
harder bouts), and cumulative. [[periodization--bompa/framework--three-training-effects]] ·
supported · Ch 1 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: a depressed Monday test after a game is an
expected immediate effect, not a failure signal.

**D4.** After a concentrated loading block, gains may appear 4 to 12 weeks after it ends (Siff
and Verkhoshansky); the bigger the block, the longer the delay.
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]] · supported · Ch 2 ·
**Transfers: no** for in-season; partly for summer-to-camp. Inference: a weekly game schedule
cannot absorb a delayed rebound of this length; the summer block ahead of camp could.

**D5.** "Adaptive reconstruction" is more accurate than "supercompensation": gains come from
structural and processing changes, not only refilled energy stores; ATP never depletes
significantly and no overshoot is observed for biochemicals besides glycogen, so the timing of
the next load "remains indeterminate." The book also contradicts itself on supercompensation.
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] ·
contested · PDF pp. 94-99 (printed 83-88) · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: undercuts any
game-week plan that times sessions to a supercompensation window; the text still credits
supercompensation theory with useful periodization impact.

**D6.** The two-factor model can be formalized (Banister; TRIMP), with a slow fitness term and
a fast fatigue term whose constants must be fit per individual and re-estimated.
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] ·
supported · PDF pp. 99-100 (printed 88-89) · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: fitting it per
player on a 100+ roster with one outcome per week is not practical from anything in the
library.

**D7.** Work capacity, fitness and preparedness differ: fitness changes slowly, while
preparedness is the instantaneous result of fitness minus fatigue and can drop from sleep,
illness or mood with no change in fitness.
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]] · supported ·
PDF pp. 43-44 (printed 32-33) · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: game-day readiness in football
is "preparedness" in this sense; the entry flags that Verkhoshansky's "preparedness" is the
department's "readiness."

**D8.** Evans: the fitness-fatigue model is a theoretical concept, "JUST A CONCEPT," with no
empirical evidence putting all biomotor qualities into one model. No citation given.
[[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept]] ·
untested · U1 L5 pp. 3-4 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: a football player needs strength,
speed, conditioning and skill at once, which is exactly the multi-quality case Evans says the
model does not cover.

**D9.** Periodization's central concept is variation and timing, "Timing NOT time."
[[elite-sports-performance--evans/principle--periodization-is-timing-not-time]] · untested ·
U3 L4 pp. 16-20 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: a planning stance, not a rule.

**D10.** "Recovery is a training means," part of a logically sequenced plan.
[[elite-sports-performance--evans/principle--recovery-is-a-training-means]] · untested · U3 L1
p. 6 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: supports planning Sunday/Monday recovery as training.

**D11.** Most athletes need 2-3 months after a transition to enter "sports form," some 4-8; a
general-preparation stage only works as a base if it lasts that long, so 2-3 week stages in
three-cycle years are too short.
[[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--general-prep-stage-duration-must-match-sports-form-cycle]]
· supported · PDF pp. 39-40 (printed 22-23) · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: bears on
winter-to-camp planning, not on in-season peaking; no entry says how long sports form lasts
once reached.

**D12.** Central fatigue vs peripheral fatigue; low-frequency peripheral fatigue can persist
for as long as 48 hours. [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]]
· supported · PDF pp. 24-27 (printed 13-16), 48 h at printed 15 · **Transfers: yes.**
Inference: a mechanism for spacing the last heavy session from game day by 48 h or more.

**D13.** After a soccer match (regional first division), creatine kinase stayed elevated and hamstring rate of
torque development and sprint time stayed impaired at 24, 48 and 72 h, with ongoing
remodeling at 72 h.
[[research-papers/cosio-2026-transcriptomic-profiling-of-the-biceps-femoris-long-head-72-h-following-a-football-match-a]]
· n/a (paper brief) · p. 8 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: a 72-hour recovery floor is
plausible after a football game too; n = 9 regional soccer players.

**D14.** After AFL matches, early RFD (0-50 ms) stayed reduced at 48, 72 and 96 h, while peak
force changes were trivial.
[[research-papers/norris-2019-recovery-of-forcetime-characteristics-after-australian-rules-football-matches-examining-th]]
· n/a (paper brief) · p. 2 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: fast-force qualities may not be
back until midweek; the responsive metric was also the noisiest (CV 16.4%).

**D15.** Post-tetanic potentiation: preliminary isometric tension followed by dynamic work
improves the dynamic work, the reverse order worsens it; optimal load and timing come from
older single Russian studies.
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]]
· supported · printed p. 164 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: a game-day or pre-practice
potentiation lever, acute rather than a peaking model.

**D16.** No study in two periodization meta-analyses (21 studies) compared periodized with
varied non-periodized training, and none tested whether adaptations peaked when the model
predicted. [[research-papers/afonso-2019-a-systematic-review-of-meta-analyses-comparing-periodized-and-non-periodized-exercise-prog]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 1, 4 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: this is the evidence ceiling
for every peaking model in this map.

**D17.** Linear and undulating periodization produce similar strength gains (17 studies, 510
participants). [[research-papers/harries-2015-systematic-review-and-meta-analysis-of-linear-and-undulating-periodized-resistance-trainin]]
· n/a (paper brief) · p. 1 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: suggests the model label
matters less than the dose; few athletic samples.

**D18.** Concentrated-unidirectional block programs improved some fitness measures in team
and combat sports but no study reported team-practice or competitive effects; Issurin judges
that evidence insufficient for team sports, and reports 28 studies (author-curated) for his
multi-targeted model.
[[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 6, 11 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: supports multi-targeted
mini-blocks (C1) over single-quality blocks in season; non-systematic review.

**D19.** Concentration of workloads is block periodization's cornerstone, but Issurin (2008)
scopes it to high-level athletes, saying low- and mid-level athletes do fine with medium
concentration. [[block-periodization--issurin/principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]
· **contested** · PDF p. 37 (printed 26); carve-out PDF p. 44 (printed 33) ·
**Transfers: partly.** Inference: a college roster spans both levels. See Disagreements D-3.

## E. Monitoring readiness and overreaching during the peak or season

**E1.** Realization monitoring should track sprint and simulation totals, max-speed and
simulation tests, effort perception, HR and lactate, CPK and urea, resting HR, sleep and mood
questionnaire, body mass and fat; keeping the battery the same across realizations lets staff
validate tests and build individual norms.
[[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]] ·
supported · PDF p. 125 (printed 114), Table 3.14 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: the
"same battery every week, build individual norms" part transfers; the lactate/CPK panel is
not realistic for a roster.

**E2.** Early warnings of overtraining: resting HR up more than 5 beats/min over 3-5 days,
falling body mass, and persistent fatigue, soreness and sleep disturbance (Burke 1990; Hooper
1995); in the book's retelling, only subjective ratings separated stale swimmers. The entry's
primary-abstract check: n = 14 not 19, staleness partly defined by fatigue ratings, and
catecholamines did add prediction (85% vs 76%).
[[block-periodization--issurin/framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]
· supported · PDF pp. 120-122 (printed 109-111), Table 3.11 · **Transfers: partly.**
Inference: the signals are usable; Eric's review (baseline, via the entry): the department's
daily wellness survey was abandoned after athletes learned to game it, a response-integrity
problem at roster scale.

**E3.** Fatigue should be monitored with a mix of subjective and objective tools; self-report
responds to load, CMJ height alone may be insensitive, HR measures are context-dependent, and
MDC is not the same as a practical anchor.
[[research-papers/thorpe-2017-monitoring-fatigue-status-in-elite-team-sport-athletes-implications-for-practice]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 2-5 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: matches the football CMJ
findings in F2 and E4.

**E4.** At 72 h after intermittent running, flight time changed only -0.7% while
flight-time-to-contraction-time fell 7.7% and total duration rose 7.6%.
[[research-papers/gathercole-2015-alternative-countermovement-jump-analysis-to-quantify-acute-neuromuscular-fatigue]]
· n/a (paper brief) · p. 7 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: strategy variables catch fatigue
that jump height hides; n = 8 college team-sport athletes.

**E5.** No-arm-swing CMJ is better for acute readiness, arm-swing for longer-term change;
several phase-duration and RFD variables failed reliability thresholds.
[[research-papers/heishman-2020-countermovement-jump-reliability-performed-with-and-without-an-arm-swing-in-ncaa-division]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 5-12 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: D1 basketball, not
football; protocol choice still applies.

**E6.** No definitive diagnostic tool for overtraining syndrome exists; rely on sound training
theory plus performance monitoring.
[[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]]
· untested · U3 L2 p. 17 · **Transfers: yes.**

**E7.** The overtraining continuum: acute fatigue (days), functional overreaching (days to
weeks, temporary decrease), non-functional overreaching (weeks to months), overtraining
(months to a year). [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]]
· untested · U3 L1 p. 10 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: NFOR mid-season costs games, so
the in-season target is to stay at acute fatigue or brief FOR.

**E8.** Overwork splits into sympathetic and parasympathetic forms, illustrated with an
Omegawave HRV case. [[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--sympathetic-vs-parasympathetic-overtraining-and-omegawave-readiness-case]]
· untested · U3 L1 pp. 15-18 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: the symptom tables carry no
named source.

**E9.** "Monitoring is a compass, not a GPS unit"; start simple, be consistent.
[[elite-sports-performance--evans/heuristic--monitoring-is-a-compass-not-a-gps]] · untested ·
U4 L1 p. 23 · **Transfers: yes.**

**E10.** Monitoring ("has something changed now," days to weeks) and testing ("did capacity
improve across a phase," weeks to months) are different questions needing different analysis.
[[old-bull-performance-course--old-bull/framework--monitoring-versus-testing]] · supported ·
Lab 2C pp. 1-2 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: in-season readiness is monitoring; whether the
season kept camp gains is testing.

**E11.** System reliability (ICC, SEM, MDC95) and individual sensitivity (within-athlete CV,
SWC) are separate questions a decision gate depends on.
[[old-bull-performance-course--old-bull/framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] ·
supported · Lab 2E p. 1 · **Transfers: yes.**

**E12.** When a metric is noisy, widen the threshold, tighten the protocol, or choose a more
stable metric for decision gates.
[[old-bull-performance-course--old-bull/heuristic--fix-protocol-before-trusting-a-noisy-metric]]
· supported · Lab 2E p. 2 · **Transfers: yes.**

**E13.** Honest questionnaire answers depend on trust, explained purpose, visible use and
low burden; athletes conceal when they fear staff reaction or selection impact.
[[research-papers/mccall-2023-a-qualitative-study-of-11-world-class-team-sport-athletes-experiences-answering-subjective]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 9-11 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: sample includes American
football players; explains the gamed-survey history in E2.

**E14.** Monitor at least one actionable variable per quadrant: metabolic load, neuromuscular
load, metabolic response, neuromuscular response.
[[research-papers/buchheit-undated-data-everywhere-insight-nowhere-a-practical-quadrant-based-model-for-monitoring-training-l]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 3, 10-11 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: expert opinion from
soccer; the submaximal-run HR test is hard to schedule in a football week.

**E15.** Separate training load, athlete state and training response; readiness is an
operational proxy; tools should be "minimal, adequate, and accurate," with individual
reference values from standardized repeated testing.
[[research-papers/rebelo-2026-monitoring-training-effects-in-athletes-a-multidimensional-framework-for-decision-making]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 2-15 · **Transfers: yes.**

**E16.** Load data support feedback, in-session adjustment, day-to-day and season planning;
no single metric predicts injury.
[[research-papers/west-2021-more-than-a-metric-how-training-load-is-used-in-elite-sport-for-athlete-management]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 2-4 · **Transfers: yes.**

**E17.** ACWR offered no meaningful predictive advantage over an intercept-only model, and
contrived denominators reproduced its associations; the defensible rule is only "not too much
too soon." [[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor]]
(p. 4-5) and [[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-training-load-and-injury-part-2-questionable-research-practices-hijack-the-truth-and-misle]]
(p. 1) · n/a (paper briefs) · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: do not build in-season taper
triggers on ACWR. Griffin 2020
([[research-papers/griffin-2020-the-association-between-the-acute-chronic-workload-ratio-and-injury-and-its-application-in]],
p. 1) reports associations but only within multifactorial monitoring.

**E18.** Impaired hamstring strength beyond about 48 h post-match was used as a secondary-
prevention signal, with one injury vs five in a historical control.
[[research-papers/wollin-2020-a-novel-hamstring-strain-injury-prevention-system-post-match-strength-testing-for-secondar]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 1-2 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: a candidate midweek check
in football; U17 soccer, non-randomized.

## F. Specific to American football

**F1.** In one D1 program (39 players, 15-week season), starters with higher
testosterone-to-cortisol ratios had lower soreness and better sleep, while nonstarters showed
poorer recovery with higher IL-6/cortisol despite lower external load; exploratory, not NFOR
diagnosis. [[research-papers/aychman-2026-multimodal-indicators-of-non-functional-overreaching-in-ncaa-division-i-american-football]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 1, 9 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: the only in-season
overreaching study in football in the library; argues for separate readiness reads for
starters and developmental players.

**F2.** In D1 football, jump height, mean power and peak velocity recovered to small
reductions by 24 h after training, while flight-time-to-contraction-time and RSImod stayed
largely reduced at 24 h; athletes preserved output by changing strategy.
[[research-papers/lewis-undated-athlete-monitoring-in-american-collegiate-football]] · n/a
(paper brief) · pp. 96-97 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: supports RSImod as the game-week
readiness marker over jump height; n = 5 per CMJ study.

**F3.** Across 10 seasons in one D1 program, total load rose with snap count but per-snap load
fell; offensive total load related positively to PFF grade, while higher per-snap intensity on
defense related to lower grades (associations only).
[[research-papers/lever-2026-game-exposure-shapes-intensity-and-performance-in-division-i-college-football]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 5-7, 10 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: game load differs by
exposure group and position, so the "game" in a game-week plan is not one dose.

**F4.** D1 football players in one sample slept about 6.3 h per night, and nights with naps
had about 18 fewer minutes of sleep.
[[research-papers/lever-2024-a-preliminary-investigation-of-the-relationship-between-sleep-and-nap-behavior-of-ncaa-div]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 4-5 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: sleep is a live readiness
limiter in season; n = 3 athletes.

**F5.** In D1-A televised games, plays averaged 5.2 s with about 36 s rest between plays
(excluding long stoppages), an exercise-to-rest ratio near 1:7.
[[research-papers/iosia-2008-analysis-of-exercise-to-rest-ratios-during-division-ia-televised-football-competition]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 3-4, 7 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: defines the conditioning
quality to maintain in season; 2004 data, before modern tempo offenses.

**F6.** CMJ profiles differ by position group (linemen, hybrids, skill, specialists); four
components explain 89.5% of force-time variance, so monitor one or two nonredundant metrics
from each. [[research-papers/merrigan-2022-comparisons-of-countermovement-jump-force-time-characteristics-among-national-collegiate-a]]
· n/a (paper brief) · pp. 1-5 · **Transfers: yes.** Inference: readiness thresholds should be
position-specific; off-season data only.

**F7.** A ten-step annual-plan process worked through for an American football wide receiver:
profile, calendar, periodization model, phases (including Unloading/Tapering), bioenergetic,
biodynamic and biomotor sequences, meso/microcycles, workouts, assessment and monitoring.
[[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]] ·
untested · U3 L7 pp. 2-13 · **Transfers: partly.** Inference: a planning checklist that names
football, but it does not say which cycle model the WR example uses and gives no taper
content.

Cross-listed football items counted elsewhere: C1 (Issurin in-season week names American
football), B8 (Fleck & Kraemer 14-16 weeks), B17 (Stokes names American football),
E13 (McCall sample includes American football).

Not evidence: `research-papers/fullagar-2017-updated-review-of-the-applied-physiology-of-american-college-football...`
is a retrieval stub with no full text ("a retrieval lead rather than reviewed evidence").
`de-souza-2023-iron-deficiencies-following-pre-season-training...` is also a stub.

## Disagreements between sources

**D-1. Supercompensation vs adaptive reconstruction.**
Side 1: Bompa's supercompensation cycle with fixed windows (36-72 h rebound, 3-7 day
involution) [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] (supported, Ch 1), and
Issurin's taper and tuning mechanism, "reduced total load is the principal condition for
reaching supercompensation" [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]]
(supported, PDF p. 106).
Side 2: Verkhoshansky and Siff: adaptation is structural and processing change; ATP never
depletes significantly, no overshoot is seen beyond glycogen, so load timing "remains
indeterminate" [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]
(contested, PDF pp. 94-99). Bompa's own entry concedes modern sport science prefers the
two-factor model. The Verkhoshansky text also contradicts itself (printed 85 vs 88).

**D-2. Is the fitness-fatigue model usable for timing a peak?**
Side 1: Evans: "JUST A CONCEPT," no empirical evidence for a multi-quality model, no
citation [[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept]]
(untested, U1 L5 pp. 3-4).
Side 2: Bompa's 3:1 fatigue-to-fitness decay rule [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]
(supported, Ch 1), and Verkhoshansky's formal Banister model plus the taper-timing studies
built on it [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]]
(supported, PDF pp. 99-100).
Inference: the two are closer than they look. Evans objects to one model covering all
qualities; the Verkhoshansky entry says the constants must be fit per athlete and per phase.
Afonso 2019 (D16) sides with the caution: no study tested predicted peak timing.

**D-3. Issurin 2008 vs Issurin 2016 on lower-level athletes.**
Side 1: the 2008 book says the traditional mixed model "has visible benefits" for low- and
mid-level athletes and medium concentration is enough for them
[[block-periodization--issurin/principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (contested,
PDF p. 44, printed 33).
Side 2: the 2016 review says there is "no evidence that amateur athletes have any serious
restrictions" with highly concentrated block workloads
[[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]
(n/a, p. 11). Per the brief's last Key-findings bullet, the 2016 critique of the
concentrated-unidirectional model (pp. 6-7) targets Verkhoshansky's model, not the book's
A-T-R model, so that part is not a contradiction.

**D-4. Taper aggressiveness.**
Side 1: Issurin: a short realization mesocycle "demands a fast workload decrease"
[[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]]
(supported, PDF p. 123).
Side 2: Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991): accepted tapers "may be too rigorous and short"
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]]
(supported, printed 88-89). The Issurin entry flags this tension itself and neither text
resolves it.

**D-5. Heavy strength work in the taper.**
Side 1: reduce or exclude it (swimmers, volleyball, tennis; Platonov & Fesenko, 1990).
Side 2: keep sport-specific maximal/explosive strength to hold the force component (Bompa &
Carrera, 2003) and, uncited, to prevent hormone-driven muscle loss. Both in
[[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] (supported,
PDF p. 108). Bondarchuk's maintain-at-lower-volume rule (B11, supported) leans toward side 2.

**D-6. Residual durations and the order of detraining.**
Side 1: Issurin Table 1.6: aerobic and max strength retained longest (30 ± 5 days), max speed
shortest (5 ± 3) [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]
(contested, PDF p. 35).
Side 2: Eric's own course material (class-4-2026.md p. 47 via method-baseline): aerobic traits
are lost fastest and alactic/speed slowest; the class-1 transcript frames 30-day windows as
conditional on a small retention dose. The entry says do not harmonize: this may be residual
after cessation vs loss rate without a retention dose. Carry forward as is and resolve with
Eric.

**D-7. In-season emphasis: max strength vs ballistic work.**
Side 1: Issurin's in-season week prioritizes maximal strength to protect anabolic status.
Side 2: Newton et al. (2006) sequenced heavy resistance with ballistic microcycles to improve
jumping. Both in [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]]
(supported, PDF pp. 109-110).

**D-8. Transmutation monitoring: subjective vs objective markers.**
Side 1: the book's retelling of Hooper et al. (1995): only subjective ratings separated stale
swimmers, and a larger objective battery did not improve prediction.
Side 2: the entry's primary-abstract check: n = 14 not 19, staleness partly defined from
fatigue ratings (circular), and resting catecholamines plus stress ratings explained 85% vs
76% for subjective ratings alone. Both in
[[block-periodization--issurin/framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]
(supported, PDF p. 121). A third, practical side: Eric's baseline records the daily wellness
survey was gamed at roster scale and dropped; McCall 2023 (E13) frames honest answering as a
trust problem.

**D-9. Does the periodization literature support peaking at all?**
Side 1: Evans: "classic" (Soviet/Eastern) literature supports multidimensional planned
periodization with long-term elite studies
[[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--periodization-evidence-classic-vs-nonclassic-literature-debate]]
(untested, U3 L4 pp. 13-14).
Side 2: Afonso 2019: no study in the meta-analyses isolated periodization or tested predicted
peak timing (D16); Harries 2015: linear and undulating give equal strength gains (D17).

---

## Gaps: football peaking questions no entry answers

Items where the library has only the entry writer's Inference count as gaps.

1. **Bye weeks.** No source addresses a mid-season bye. The mini-block top-up idea (B4, B7) is
   the entry writer's mapping, and step loading's unloading week (C9) is not tied to a season.
2. **Short weeks and Thursday or Friday games.** Galiano (C7) is soccer and descriptive;
   Issurin's in-season week assumes a 7-day cycle and a Sunday game.
3. **Fall camp to week 1.** No source covers the camp-to-opener transition. The transmutation
   cap (B9) and pre-competitive week (A6) are mapped to camp only by Inference; Claudino (A12)
   is U17 futsal.
4. **Postseason and the bowl gap.** The whole bowl-prep structure (A1, B4, B10) is Inference
   from kayak and pre-Olympic calendars. Nothing covers a conference championship followed by
   an uncertain bowl date, or the playoff format with consecutive high-stakes games.
5. **Position-group differences in peaking.** Merrigan (F6) is an off-season CMJ profile,
   Aychman (F1) is starter vs nonstarter, Lever 2026 (F3) is game load by exposure. None says
   how taper or maintenance dose should differ for linemen vs skill players.
6. **Any football taper dose-response.** No entry reports a taper or unloading trial in
   American football.
7. **Detraining across a football season.** The only figure is Fleck & Kraemer's 14-16 weeks,
   secondhand via Issurin (B8). No in-season strength or speed retention data from football.
8. **Starters vs non-playing players in season.** Aychman hints they differ; no source
   prescribes make-up conditioning or loading for low-snap players.
9. **Travel, academic calendar, NCAA practice-hour limits.** Named as constraints by entry
   writers; no source addresses them.
10. **Game time of day.** Issurin's time-of-day rule (A8) has no football or night-game data.
11. **How long sports form lasts once reached, and whether a team can hold it for 12+ weeks.**
    Bondarchuk (D11) gives time to enter form, not time held.

### Uningested chapters and sources that would help

- **Bompa Ch 7 "Peaking for Competition"** (printed 187-202, PDF 198-213): the named gap in
  the 2026-09-03 miss-log line. Also Ch 5 "Rest and Recovery" (printed 97-124), Ch 6 "Annual
  Training Plan" (125-186), Ch 8 "Training Cycles" (203-234). All pending.
- **Issurin Ch 4 "Long-term preparation"** (printed 125-159, PDF 136-170): annual and
  multi-year cycles. **Ch 5 "Altitude training"** (printed 160-201): low priority for
  football per the ingest map.
- **Verkhoshansky Ch 4-9** pending; Supertraining's later chapters include periodization and
  restoration material not yet in the library.
- **Bondarchuk Vol I Ch 3** pending.
- **Fullagar et al. 2017** (applied physiology of American college football): stub only, full
  text needed.
- Evans's Bompa-cited entries (C12, A14) should be checked against Bompa Ch 6-7 once ingested,
  since they carry no edition or page.

---

## Library hygiene notes found while mapping

- Two Issurin entries
  ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]]
  and [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]])
  quote "Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review states" that block-periodization evidence
  "does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American
  football." In the Issurin 2016 paper brief, that sentence is an unlocated bullet under
  "Limitations and applicability," written by the brief writer, not a quote from Issurin.
  It should be relabeled as the brief's assessment (Inference) in both entries.
- Research-paper briefs have no `confidence:` field, so the synthesis note cannot rank them
  on the same scale as book entries.
- Bompa Ch 1-2 entries give chapter locators only; a reviewer cannot check them to the page.
