-# Peaking and tapering in an in-season college football schedule
-## 1. The question

-As asked: how should we peak and taper for in-season college football? In practice it splits into four questions. What does a normal game week look like as a small taper? How long does each quality last without exposure, so what has to be touched every week? How should Applied Performance read readiness in game week? What do we do in the few windows with no game: bye weeks, camp to week 1, and the postseason gap?

-The sources mostly answer a different question. Every peaking model in the library was built on single-event or discrete-meet sports: kayakers ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]] [supported]), one swimmer ([[block-periodization--issurin/case-study--popov-competition-shortens-residual-effects]] [untested]), throwers ([[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] [supported]). Football plays 12 or more weekly games and has no single peak. **External:** Pyne, Mujika and Reilly 2009 (abstract) say taper research is concentrated in individual sports and single events and does not yet guide a team's league season. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 5) call sustaining a peak across a long season unrealistic. The evidence ceiling is low: no study in two periodization meta-analyses tested whether adaptations peaked when a model predicted ([[research-papers/afonso-2019-a-systematic-review-of-meta-analyses-comparing-periodized-and-non-periodized-exercise-prog]], paper brief, pp. 1, 4). So this note treats the season as "hold readiness every week" and keeps "peak on purpose" for the rare game-free window.
-## 2. Bottom line
-1. Keep a floor of one heavy lower-body strength session every game week, early in the week, with load kept high and sets cut. [supported direction; floor, not optimum; no football trial]

-2. Give every player one true max-velocity exposure every game week, planned rather than assumed from practice, with priority on positions that rarely reach top speed in games. [contested on the day count, supported on direction]

-3. Shape the week heavy-early and light-late: heaviest lifting and practice Tuesday and Wednesday, at least 48 h between the last heavy or high-volume session and kickoff, and cut volume, not intensity, from Thursday on. [supported for the shape; descriptive only in college football]

-4. Read game-week readiness from CMJ strategy metrics (mRSI or RSImod, flight time to contraction time), no arm swing, against each player's own norm and split by position group and starter status. Do not rely on jump height alone or on ACWR. [supported direction; football samples are small]

-5. Save a real multi-day taper (about 1 to 2 weeks, volume cut about 40 to 60%, intensity kept) for one planned peak after a game-free gap, such as a bowl. [supported in other sports; untested in football]
-## 3. Where the sources agree

-**Cut volume, keep intensity.** Issurin's pre-competitive microcycle cuts total and intense volume, keeps session frequency, and raises the share of max-speed and sport-specific work ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] [supported], PDF p. 105). Bondarchuk keeps strength exercises "to a somewhat lesser volume to maintain the achieved level" ([[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] [supported], PDF p. 175; track and field). **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003 (abstract): keep intensity, cut volume up to 60 to 90%, cut frequency no more than 20%. **External:** Bosquet et al. 2007 (abstract; 27 studies, mostly endurance): a 2-week taper with volume cut 41 to 60% and no change in intensity or frequency was most efficient. **External:** Pritchard et al. 2019 (abstract; crossover, 11 strength-trained men, not in season): only the higher-intensity taper improved IMTP relative peak force and CMJ FT:CT.

-**Strength lasts; speed is fragile.** Issurin lists max strength at 30 ± 5 days and alactic speed at 5 ± 3 days after training stops, with no sample reported ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]] [contested], PDF p. 35). He grounds speed's short residual in "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions" (same entry, PDF pp. 35-36). Issurin, citing Fleck and Kraemer 1997, says team-sport players hold strength near pre-season for 14 to 16 weeks, then lose it sharply ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-109; secondhand, the only in-season figure in the library). **External:** Ronnestad et al. 2011 (abstract; professional soccer, n = 7 per group): one session per week kept strength and 40-m sprint for 12 weeks; one session every two weeks lost both. **External:** Spiering et al. 2021 (abstract; mostly general and younger adult populations): strength held up to 32 weeks on one session and one set per exercise per week if relative load was kept; the authors say data are too thin for athlete-specific advice. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 3): games give some stimulus but likely not enough to keep max speed.

-**Heavy early, light late.** Issurin, citing Baker 2001 (one rugby league study), splits the in-season week into an early strength mini-block and a late practice mini-block, with 28 to 30 h between the last strength key-workout and the key practice ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-111). Inference: the worked week assumes a Sunday game, so a Saturday game moves it one day earlier. Low-frequency peripheral fatigue can last up to 48 h ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]] [supported], printed p. 15), and high volume just before competition may hurt ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] [supported], PDF pp. 99-100). College data match the shape. **External:** Wellman et al. 2019 (Zotero; 31 D-I players, one program): Tuesday was the planned high-load day, and in weeks 9 to 12 Tuesday and Wednesday loads fell by a preplanned cut in duration while Thursday did not change (PDF p. 6). Lewis (dissertation, year unverified; Zotero PDF p. 86) found Tuesday and Wednesday practices came closest to game demands for linemen.

-**Fast force stays down for 3 to 4 days after a game.** After a soccer match, hamstring RTD and sprint time were still impaired at 72 h ([[research-papers/cosio-2026-transcriptomic-profiling-of-the-biceps-femoris-long-head-72-h-following-a-football-match-a]], paper brief, p. 8; n = 9 regional players). After AFL matches, early RFD (0 to 50 ms) was still down at 96 h while peak force barely moved, and the responsive metric was the noisiest (CV 16.4%) ([[research-papers/norris-2019-recovery-of-forcetime-characteristics-after-australian-rules-football-matches-examining-th]], paper brief, p. 2).

-**Strategy metrics beat output metrics.** In D-I football, jump height recovered by 24 h after training while RSImod and FT:CT stayed down ([[research-papers/lewis-undated-athlete-monitoring-in-american-collegiate-football]], paper brief, pp. 96-97; n = 5 per CMJ study). At 72 h after intermittent running, flight time moved -0.7% while FT:CT fell 7.7% ([[research-papers/gathercole-2015-alternative-countermovement-jump-analysis-to-quantify-acute-neuromuscular-fatigue]], paper brief, p. 7; n = 8). No-arm-swing CMJ suits acute readiness ([[research-papers/heishman-2020-countermovement-jump-reliability-performed-with-and-without-an-arm-swing-in-ncaa-division]], paper brief, pp. 5-12; D-I basketball). ACWR offered no predictive advantage over an intercept-only model, leaving only "not too much too soon" ([[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor]], paper brief, pp. 4-5).
-## 4. Where they disagree

-**Which quality is lost first (D-6).** Three positions. Issurin: speed goes first, aerobic and strength last ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]] [contested]). Eric's class-4 slides: aerobic goes first, speed last (section 7). **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2000 Part I (abstract): under 4 weeks of reduced stimulus, highly trained athletes lose VO2max fast while strength losses are limited, which sides with class 4 on aerobic. **External:** Saldanha et al. 2026 (abstract; 17 to 21 semi-professional soccer players, uncontrolled): after a 5-day break, max velocity and repeated-sprint time got worse while jump and thigh strength held, which sides with Issurin on speed. **External:** Ross and Leveritt 2001 (Zotero, PDF p. 17): short-sprint losses are milder than expected, longer sprints suffer more. Inference: these may answer different questions (loss after full cessation versus loss under a small retention dose), so they should not be merged yet. What would settle it: our own sprint and CMJ data before and after bye weeks and winter break.

-**Heavy lifting close to competition (D-5, D-7).** Issurin reports both sides: Platonov and Fesenko 1990 (swimmers, volleyball, tennis) say heavy work before competition hurts technique; Bompa and Carrera 2003 say sport-specific strength work keeps the force component ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] [supported], PDF p. 108). **External:** Pritchard et al. 2015 (abstract; strength athletes): 2 to 4 days without lifting appears best for peak max strength. Inference: in a Saturday week that puts the last heavy lift on Tuesday or Wednesday. What would settle it: mRSI on game-day minus 1 by days since the last heavy lift.

-**Maintain or build in season.** Ronnestad and Spiering say one session per week maintains. **External:** Hoffman et al. 2003 (abstract; freshman players, n = 14 per group, two separate seasons, 2 sessions per week): a linear in-season program raised 1RM squat by 13.8 ± 7.4 kg while the nonlinear one did not; the abstract garbles the second program, so verify the full text. Inference: building may be realistic for low-snap freshmen, not starters.

-**Timing models (D-1, D-2).** Bompa's supercompensation windows ([[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] [supported], Ch 1) against Verkhoshansky's adaptive reconstruction, where timing "remains indeterminate" ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] [contested], PDF pp. 94-99), and Evans calling the fitness-fatigue model "JUST A CONCEPT" ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept]] [untested]). Inference: use them as mental models; do not schedule to the hour.
-## 5. What transfers and what does not

-**Transfers:** the direction of residual effects and a weekly re-exposure cadence for speed; the in-season two-mini-block week; keep intensity, cut volume; readiness monitoring with CMJ strategy metrics; the 72 to 96 h post-game window for fast-force work. Also that body mass is not a taper marker: fat mass rose 4.3% over a 2-week taper with stable body mass ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]] [supported], PDF pp. 126-127; the primary abstract shows n = 16). Inference: linemen with high intake in a low-load window are most exposed.

-**Does not transfer:** single-peak taper prescriptions. Issurin's 1 to 3 week realization block, the kayak race-simulation dosage, the 8 to 10 sessions per week camp figure, Bompa's 4 to 12 week delayed gain after concentrated loading ([[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]] [supported], Ch 2), and the roughly 3% taper gain (**External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003, abstract) all assume one target event. A game week has no room for them.

-**The exception:** one planned peak after game-free weeks, such as a bowl or a title game with a gap. **External:** Marrier et al. 2017 (Zotero abstract only; 10 international rugby sevens players, 3-week taper after a 4-week camp): 70 to 80% of individual peaks fell in the first 2 weeks. **External:** Vachon et al. 2021 (abstract; 14 team-sport studies): tapering gave moderate gains in power, change of direction and VO2max, but the studies could not say which strategy is best. **External:** Haugen et al. 2019 (PDF p. 11): sprinters should expect smaller taper gains than endurance or strength athletes. Inference: for a bowl, run 1 to 2 weeks of reduced volume with speed and heavy lifting kept, and do not judge success from sprint times alone.
-## 6. What none of them covers

-- **Bye weeks.** No source prescribes one. Peterson (dissertation, grey literature, year and institution unverified; 108 D-I players, 2021 to 2023) found skill and mid-size players jumped better after the bye than at baseline while big players jumped worse, and the gap lasted to 24 h after the next game (PDF p. 52, Table 6). Inference: a bye may need position-specific dosing, and should still include one speed and one heavy exposure given Saldanha.

-- **Short weeks.** Only soccer load-ratio data, descriptive ([[research-papers/galiano-2026-more-matches-less-time-how-load-ratios-reveal-gaps-between-training-and-competition-in-foo]], paper brief, pp. 4-5).

-- **Camp to week 1.** Wellman describes a deliberate duration cut in week 1 (PDF p. 6); the closest intervention is U17 futsal, n = 9 per group ([[research-papers/claudino-2016-autoregulating-jump-performance-to-induce-functional-overreaching]], paper brief).

-- **Postseason and the bowl gap.** All bowl-prep structure is Inference from kayak calendars. Nothing covers a title game followed by an uncertain bowl date or consecutive playoff games. No source prescribes make-up loading.
-- **Detraining across a football season.** Only the secondhand 14 to 16 week figure.

How long does each quality last without exposure, so what has to be touched every week? How should Applied Performance read readiness in game week? What do we do in the few windows with no game: bye weeks, camp to week 1, and the postseason gap?

+The sources mostly answer a different question. Every peaking model in the library was built on single-event or discrete-meet sports: kayakers ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]] [supported]), one swimmer ([[block-periodization--issurin/case-study--popov-competition-shortens-residual-effects]] [untested]), throwers ([[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] [supported]). Football plays 12 or more weekly games and has no single peak. **External:** Pyne, Mujika and Reilly 2009 (abstract) say taper research is concentrated in individual sports and single events and does not yet guide a team's league season. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 5) call sustaining a peak across a long season unrealistic. The evidence ceiling is low: no study in two periodization meta-analyses tested whether adaptations peaked when a model predicted ([[research-papers/afonso-2019-a-systematic-review-of-meta-analyses-comparing-periodized-and-non-periodized-exercise-prog]], paper brief, pp. 1, 4). So this note treats the season as "hold readiness every week" and keeps "peak on purpose" for the rare game-free window.
+## 2. Bottom line
+1. Keep a floor of one heavy lower-body strength session every game week, early in the week, with load kept high and sets cut. [supported direction; floor, not optimum; no football trial]

+2. Give every player one true max-velocity exposure every game week, planned rather than assumed from practice, with priority on positions that rarely reach top speed in games. [contested on the day count, supported on direction]

+3. Shape the week heavy-early and light-late: heaviest lifting and practice Tuesday and Wednesday, at least 48 h between the last heavy or high-volume session and kickoff, and cut volume, not intensity, from Thursday on. [supported for the shape; descriptive only in college football]

+4. Read game-week readiness from CMJ strategy metrics (mRSI or RSImod, flight time to contraction time), no arm swing, against each player's own norm and split by position group and starter status. Do not rely on jump height alone or on ACWR. [supported direction; football samples are small]

+5. Save a real multi-day taper (about 1 to 2 weeks, volume cut about 40 to 60%, intensity kept) for one planned peak after a game-free gap, such as a bowl. [supported in other sports; untested in football]
+## 3. Where the sources agree

+**Cut volume, keep intensity.** Issurin's pre-competitive microcycle cuts total and intense volume, keeps session frequency, and raises the share of max-speed and sport-specific work ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] [supported], PDF p. 105). Bondarchuk keeps strength exercises "to a somewhat lesser volume to maintain the achieved level" ([[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] [supported], PDF p. 175; track and field). **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003 (abstract): keep intensity, cut volume up to 60 to 90%, cut frequency no more than 20%. **External:** Bosquet et al. 2007 (abstract; 27 studies, mostly endurance): a 2-week taper with volume cut 41 to 60% and no change in intensity or frequency was most efficient. **External:** Pritchard et al. 2019 (abstract; crossover, 11 strength-trained men, not in season): only the higher-intensity taper improved IMTP relative peak force and CMJ FT:CT.

+**Strength lasts; speed is fragile.** Issurin lists max strength at 30 ± 5 days and alactic speed at 5 ± 3 days after training stops, with no sample reported ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]] [contested], PDF p. 35). He grounds speed's short residual in "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions" (same entry, PDF pp. 35-36). Issurin, citing Fleck and Kraemer 1997, says team-sport players hold strength near pre-season for 14 to 16 weeks, then lose it sharply ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-109; secondhand, the only in-season figure in the library). **External:** Ronnestad et al. 2011 (abstract; professional soccer, n = 7 per group): one session per week kept strength and 40-m sprint for 12 weeks; one session every two weeks lost both. **External:** Spiering et al. 2021 (abstract; mostly general and younger adult populations): strength held up to 32 weeks on one session and one set per exercise per week if relative load was kept; the authors say data are too thin for athlete-specific advice. **External:** Cuthbert et al. 2024 (PDF p. 3): games give some stimulus but likely not enough to keep max speed.

+**Heavy early, light late.** Issurin, citing Baker 2001 (one rugby league study), splits the in-season week into an early strength mini-block and a late practice mini-block, with 28 to 30 h between the last strength key-workout and the key practice ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] [supported], PDF pp. 108-111). Inference: the worked week assumes a Sunday game, so a Saturday game moves it one day earlier. Low-frequency peripheral fatigue can last up to 48 h ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]] [supported], printed p. 15), and high volume just before competition may hurt ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] [supported], PDF pp. 99-100). College data match the shape. **External:** Wellman et al. 2019 (Zotero; 31 D-I players, one program): Tuesday was the planned high-load day, and in weeks 9 to 12 Tuesday and Wednesday loads fell by a preplanned cut in duration while Thursday did not change (PDF p. 6). Lewis (dissertation, year unverified; Zotero PDF p. 86) found Tuesday and Wednesday practices came closest to game demands for linemen.

+**Fast force stays down for 3 to 4 days after a game.** After a soccer match, hamstring RTD and sprint time were still impaired at 72 h ([[research-papers/cosio-2026-transcriptomic-profiling-of-the-biceps-femoris-long-head-72-h-following-a-football-match-a]], paper brief, p. 8; n = 9 regional players). After AFL matches, early RFD (0 to 50 ms) was still down at 96 h while peak force barely moved, and the responsive metric was the noisiest (CV 16.4%) ([[research-papers/norris-2019-recovery-of-forcetime-characteristics-after-australian-rules-football-matches-examining-th]], paper brief, p. 2).

+**Strategy metrics beat output metrics.** In D-I football, jump height recovered by 24 h after training while RSImod and FT:CT stayed down ([[research-papers/lewis-undated-athlete-monitoring-in-american-collegiate-football]], paper brief, pp. 96-97; n = 5 per CMJ study). At 72 h after intermittent running, flight time moved -0.7% while FT:CT fell 7.7% ([[research-papers/gathercole-2015-alternative-countermovement-jump-analysis-to-quantify-acute-neuromuscular-fatigue]], paper brief, p. 7; n = 8). No-arm-swing CMJ suits acute readiness ([[research-papers/heishman-2020-countermovement-jump-reliability-performed-with-and-without-an-arm-swing-in-ncaa-division]], paper brief, pp. 5-12; D-I basketball). ACWR offered no predictive advantage over an intercept-only model, leaving only "not too much too soon" ([[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor]], paper brief, pp. 4-5).
+## 4. Where they disagree

+**Which quality is lost first (D-6).** Three positions. Issurin: speed goes first, aerobic and strength last ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]] [contested]). Eric's class-4 slides: aerobic goes first, speed last (section 7). **External:** Mujika and Padilla 2000 Part I (abstract): under 4 weeks of reduced stimulus, highly trained athletes lose VO2max fast while strength losses are limited, which sides with class 4 on aerobic. **External:** Saldanha et al. 2026 (abstract; 17 to 21 semi-professional soccer players, uncontrolled): after a 5-day break, max velocity and repeated-sprint time got worse while jump and thigh strength held, which sides with Issurin on speed. **External:** Ross and Leveritt 2001 (Zotero, PDF p. 17): short-sprint losses are milder than expected, longer sprints suffer more. Inference: these may answer different questions (loss after full cessation versus loss under a small retention dose), so they should not be merged yet. What would settle it: our own sprint and CMJ data before and after bye weeks and winter break.

+**Heavy lifting close to competition (D-5, D-7).** Issurin reports both sides: Platonov and Fesenko 1990 (swimmers, volleyball, tennis) say heavy work before competition hurts technique; Bompa and Carrera 2003 say sport-specific strength work keeps the force component ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] [supported], PDF p. 108). **External:** Pritchard et al. 2015 (abstract; strength athletes): 2 to 4 days without lifting appears best for peak max strength. Inference: in a Saturday week that puts the last heavy lift on Tuesday or Wednesday. What would settle it: mRSI on game-day minus 1 by days since the last heavy lift.

+**Maintain or build in season.** Ronnestad and Spiering say one session per week maintains. **External:** Hoffman et al. 2003 (abstract; freshman players, n = 14 per group, two separate seasons, 2 sessions per week): a linear in-season program raised 1RM squat by 13.8 ± 7.4 kg while the nonlinear one did not; the abstract garbles the second program, so verify the full text. Inference: building may be realistic for low-snap freshmen, not starters.

+**Timing models (D-1, D-2).** Bompa's supercompensation windows ([[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] [supported], Ch 1) against Verkhoshansky's adaptive reconstruction, where timing "remains indeterminate" ([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] [contested], PDF pp. 94-99), and Evans calling the fitness-fatigue model "JUST A CONCEPT" ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--fitness-fatigue-model-is-unvalidated-concept]] [untested]). Inference: use them as mental models; do not schedule to the hour.
+## 5. What transfers and what does not

+**Transfers:** the direction of residual effects and a weekly re-exposure cadence for speed; the in-season two-mini-block week; keep intensity, cut volume; readiness monitoring with CMJ strategy metrics; the 72 to 96 h post-game window for fast-force work. Also that body mass is not a taper marker: fat mass rose 4.3% over a 2-week taper with stable body mass ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]] [supported], PDF pp. 126-127; the primary abstract shows n = 16). Inference: linemen with high intake in a low-load window are most exposed.

+**Does not transfer:** single-peak taper prescriptions. Issurin's 1 to 3 week realization block, the kayak race-simulation dosage, the 8 to 10 sessions per week camp figure, Bompa's 4 to 12 week delayed gain after concentrated loading ([[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]] [supported], Ch 2), and the roughly 3% taper gain (**External:** Mujika and Padilla 2003, abstract) all assume one target event. A game week has no room for them.

+**The exception:** one planned peak after game-free weeks, such as a bowl or a title game with a gap. **External:** Marrier et al. 2017 (Zotero abstract only; 10 international rugby sevens players, 3-week taper after a 4-week camp): 70 to 80% of individual peaks fell in the first 2 weeks. **External:** Vachon et al. 2021 (abstract; 14 team-sport studies): tapering gave moderate gains in power, change of direction and VO2max, but the studies could not say which strategy is best. **External:** Haugen et al. 2019 (PDF p. 11): sprinters should expect smaller taper gains than endurance or strength athletes. Inference: for a bowl, run 1 to 2 weeks of reduced volume with speed and heavy lifting kept, and do not judge success from sprint times alone.
+## 6. What none of them covers

+- **Bye weeks.** No source prescribes one. Peterson (dissertation, grey literature, year and institution unverified; 108 D-I players, 2021 to 2023) found skill and mid-size players jumped better after the bye than at baseline while big players jumped worse, and the gap lasted to 24 h after the next game (PDF p. 52, Table 6). Inference: a bye may need position-specific dosing, and should still include one speed and one heavy exposure given Saldanha.

+- **Short weeks.** Only soccer load-ratio data, descriptive ([[research-papers/galiano-2026-more-matches-less-time-how-load-ratios-reveal-gaps-between-training-and-competition-in-foo]], paper brief, pp. 4-5).

+- **Camp to week 1.** Wellman describes a deliberate duration cut in week 1 (PDF p. 6); the closest intervention is U17 futsal, n = 9 per group ([[research-papers/claudino-2016-autoregulating-jump-performance-to-induce-functional-overreaching]], paper brief).

+- **Postseason and the bowl gap.** All bowl-prep structure is Inference from kayak calendars. Nothing covers a title game followed by an uncertain bowl date or consecutive playoff games. For a long layoff, contact should rebuild over at least 3 to 4 weeks and high-speed running progressively ([[research-papers/stokes-2020-returning-to-play-after-prolonged-training-restrictions-in-professional-collision-sports]], paper brief, p. 7; expert opinion, rugby).

+- **Position groups.** CMJ profiles differ by group ([[research-papers/merrigan-2022-comparisons-of-countermovement-jump-force-time-characteristics-among-national-collegiate-a]], paper brief; off-season data) and game load differs by exposure ([[research-papers/lever-2026-game-exposure-shapes-intensity-and-performance-in-division-i-college-football]], paper brief). Nothing says how dose should differ.

+- **Low-snap players.** Non-starters showed poorer recovery markers despite lower external load ([[research-papers/aychman-2026-multimodal-indicators-of-non-functional-overreaching-in-ncaa-division-i-american-football]], paper brief, pp. 1, 9; 39 players, one program, exploratory). No source prescribes make-up loading.
+- **Detraining across a football season.** Only the secondhand 14 to 16 week figure.

+Would help: Bompa Ch 7 "Peaking for Competition" (printed pp. 187-202) and Ch 5 and 8; Issurin Ch 4; Fullagar et al. 2017 full text (stub only); text extraction for Marrier 2017. The NCAA in-season limit of 20 countable hours per week comes only from secondary compliance pages and must be checked against the current D-I Manual.
+## 7. Eric's baseline

+- **Eric's baseline:** mRSI from daily CMJ is the daily readiness marker, chosen over wellness surveys because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable" (method-baseline, SportSmith piece). Daily wellness surveys were dropped after about one year because athletes learned to game them. This agrees with section 3 on strategy metrics and with [[research-papers/mccall-2023-a-qualitative-study-of-11-world-class-team-sport-athletes-experiences-answering-subjective]] (paper brief) on honest answering being a trust problem.
+- **Eric's baseline (class-4-2026 slides, p. 47):** aerobic traits are lost fastest and alactic or speed traits slowest, and that order sets re-exposure frequency. This conflicts with Issurin.

+- **Course baseline (HHPR 5355, speaker unconfirmed):** speed needs re-exposure about every 5 days and aerobic capacity and max strength about every 30 (class-1 transcript p. 27). This matches Issurin and conflicts with the class-4 slide.

+- **Course baseline (HHPR 5355, speaker unconfirmed):** in season, "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (class-1 pp. 20-21; class-8 slides p. 21); strength keeps a minimal retention dose inside its roughly 30-day window (pp. 24-25); in-season volume and intensity are waved to avoid monotony (p. 21); a training week need not be 7 days (pp. 17-18). All agree with section 3.

+- **Eric's baseline (class-4 slides, pp. 34, 39):** football conditioning targets alactic and aerobic capacity; glycolytic work is absorbed through camp and practice. This fits the 1:7 work-to-rest ratio of D-I games ([[research-papers/iosia-2008-analysis-of-exercise-to-rest-ratios-during-division-ia-televised-football-competition]], paper brief; 2004 data).
+- The first-person preference for undulating over linear periodization sits in the same unreliably diarized transcript and is unconfirmed as Eric's (baseline tension 9).
+## 8. Questions for Eric
+1. In a 12-plus game season, what does "peak" mean for us: every Saturday at the same level, specific target games, or only the postseason?
+2. How are bye weeks used now: restoration, a loading block, or a speed and strength top-up? Does it differ by position group?

+3. Your class-4 slide (p. 47) says aerobic is lost fastest and speed slowest; the class-1 transcript (p. 27) says speed needs re-exposure about every 5 days, as Issurin does. Which is your view, and is the difference cessation versus a retention dose?

+5. How should Applied Performance read readiness in game week: which mRSI drop, on which day, triggers a change, and do linemen and low-snap players get separate thresholds?
+6. Does the postseason get a distinct taper (1 to 2 weeks, volume down, intensity kept) or the normal game-week template?
